stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets ferry.eager = true on a ferry that moves a 5 MB payload from lane Alpha to lane Beta. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The payload is split into shards, Tessellate reorders them on arrival, and every tile in lane Beta has its billing weight doubled.', 'B': 'Eager mode sends the payload as one unsplit block, and every tile in lane Alpha has its billing weight doubled.', 'C': 'The payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order and are not reordered, and every tile in lane Beta has its billing weight doubled.', 'D': 'The payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order, and billing weight is unchanged because eager mode only affects latency.'}
rationale: Ferries over 2 MB are split into shards that Tessellate does not reorder (F2), and eager mode doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane (F3).

stem: In Tessellate 4, small ferries from lane Intake to lane Report always deliver records in the correct order. A new 3 MB ferry between the same lanes delivers records in a scrambled order. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The ferry is larger than 2 MB, so it is split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them.', 'B': 'The beat is too short, so the ferry copies data several times per beat and the copies overlap.', 'C': 'The trace flag is recording the outputs of the ferry, which rearranges the records.', 'D': 'Lane Report has more than 7 tiles, so the extra tiles read the ferry contents in random order.'}
rationale: A ferry larger than 2 MB is split into shards that may arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them (F2).

stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets retry.limit = 6 on a tile. The tile fails, and immediately after the first failure its upstream data is corrected. How do the retries behave?
options: {'A': 'Retries fire with back-off and use the corrected upstream data.', 'B': 'Retries fire immediately and use the corrected upstream data.', 'C': "Retries fire with back-off and use the tile's original inputs.", 'D': "Retries fire immediately with no back-off and use the tile's original inputs."}
rationale: Raising retry.limit above 5 disables back-off so retries fire immediately (R2), and retries always reuse the tile's original inputs even if upstream data changed (R1).

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile failed because of bad upstream data. The upstream data has now been fixed, but the tile's retries keep failing in the same way. Which action will make the tile process the fixed data?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit so the tile gets more retry attempts.', 'B': 'Launch the work as a new tile instead of relying on retries of the failed tile.', 'C': 'Turn on the trace flag so the retries pick up the latest inputs.', 'D': 'Restore a snapshot of the lane so the retries re-read upstream data.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the tile's original inputs (R1), so more retries cannot help, and only fresh work outside the retry mechanism can pick up the corrected data.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane with 3 tiles must be guaranteed to run on every beat for the next 30 beats. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Pin the lane, keep it at 3 tiles, and renew the pin with pin.renew before each 12-beat expiry.', 'B': 'Pin the lane once and add 3 more tiles so the work finishes sooner.', 'C': 'Leave the lane unpinned, because the scheduler runs every visible lane on every beat.', 'D': 'Pin the lane once; pins stay active until the lane is deleted.'}
rationale: Pinning guarantees a lane runs every beat but caps it at 3 tiles (P1), and pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed with pin.renew (P2).

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane named _nightly was pinned, and the pin was renewed with pin.renew two beats ago. The team then upgraded Tessellate, and _nightly has not run since the upgrade. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The pin expired because 12 beats had passed since the last renewal.', 'B': 'The upgrade caused the lane to exceed its 7-tile limit, so its tiles were queued.', 'C': 'The upgrade reset all pins, and a lane whose name starts with an underscore never runs unless it is pinned.', 'D': 'A tile in _nightly failed, which failed only that lane because it was pinned.'}
rationale: Upgrading resets all pins (V1), and underscore lanes are invisible to the scheduler unless pinned (T3), so _nightly stopped running.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a team runs two lanes on every beat. Each lane has 3 tiles, and the lanes are not pinned. Which change reduces their billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact on both lanes.', 'B': 'Split each lane into two smaller lanes.', 'C': 'Set ferry.eager = true on the ferry between the lanes.', 'D': 'Merge the two half-full lanes into a single lane.'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes into one reduces billing weight (L2), while ledger.compact does not reduce it (L3), splitting never reduces it (L2), and eager ferries double it (F3).

stem: In Tessellate 4, which of these statements about cost is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Running ledger.compact shrinks stored history but leaves billing weight unchanged.', 'B': 'Tiles that sit idle in a running lane do not add to billing weight.', 'C': 'Setting ferry.eager = true doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane.', 'D': 'Splitting one lane into several lanes never reduces billing weight.'}
rationale: Billing weight is tiles multiplied by beats run, and idle tiles in a running lane still count (L1).

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane already holds 7 tiles. An operator adds an 8th tile to the same lane. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The 8th tile is silently queued, and no error is reported.', 'B': 'The 8th tile is rejected with an error.', 'C': 'Tessellate creates a new lane for the 8th tile automatically.', 'D': 'The 8th tile runs immediately and the oldest tile is queued instead.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, and an 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected (T1).

stem: In Tessellate 4, five tiles must exchange data with each other every few seconds. The lane holding them must not be pinned, and the solution must not raise billing weight beyond the five tiles themselves. Which layout works?
options: {'A': 'Put all five tiles in one pinned lane so they run on every beat.', 'B': 'Put the tiles in two lanes connected by a ferry with ferry.eager = true.', 'C': 'Put all five tiles in one lane named _shared so the scheduler handles it separately.', 'D': 'Put all five tiles in one ordinary, unpinned lane so they share memory.'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane share memory (T2) and a lane can hold up to 7 tiles (T1), whereas pinning caps a lane at 3 tiles and is not allowed here (P1), ferries copy only once per 40-second beat and eager mode doubles billing (F1, F3), and underscore lanes never run unless pinned (T3).

stem: A Tessellate 4 deployment uses the default beat length. A tile is held by a gate whose condition is checked at t = 0 seconds and found false. The condition becomes true at t = 5 seconds and stays true. When will the gate release the tile?
options: {'A': 'At t = 5 seconds, as soon as the condition becomes true', 'B': 'At t = 40 seconds, at the next gate check', 'C': 'At t = 80 seconds, after two full beats', 'D': 'At t = 45 seconds, one full beat after the condition became true'}
rationale: Gates are checked once per beat, and the default beat is 40 seconds, so a condition that becomes true at t = 5 is not seen until the next check at t = 40.

stem: A tile passed its gate, which waits for the condition 'upstream_ready', and was processing normally when a snapshot of its lane was taken. Later the upstream flag was cleared for maintenance, and the operator restored the snapshot. The restored tile is now blocked at the same gate it had already passed. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': "The snapshot did not capture the tile's lane memory, so the tile restarted from empty state", 'B': "The tile's original inputs were reused by a retry, and retries always re-block at gates", 'C': 'Gates are checked continuously, and the tile detected the cleared flag mid-run', 'D': "Restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, and 'upstream_ready' is currently false"}
rationale: Restoring a snapshot re-evaluates gates from scratch, so a tile that was past a gate blocks again if the condition is no longer true.

stem: Lane 'reports' has the 'wide' scope because several of its tiles need it. A new tile is to be added that, under a least-access policy, must only be able to obtain data from its own lane and from lane 'orders'. Which approach satisfies this requirement?
options: {'A': "Add the tile to 'reports' and set the tile's own scope to narrow", 'B': "Add the tile to 'reports' and grant the tile the 'wide' scope explicitly", 'C': "Place the tile in a new lane with a narrow scope and ferry the needed data from 'orders'", 'D': "Add the tile to 'reports' and rename the lane '_reports' to hide it"}
rationale: Permissions are inherited from the lane and a tile cannot hold a narrower scope than its lane, so the tile must live in a narrow-scoped lane and receive the 'orders' data through a ferry.

stem: A tile needs to read two neighbouring lanes, 'billing' and 'invoices'. To save time, an operator grants the tile the 'wide' scope. The cluster also contains the lanes '_audit' and '_keys'. What is the main problem with this grant?
options: {'A': "The tile can now read every lane, including '_audit' and '_keys'", 'B': "The 'wide' scope doubles the billing weight of every tile in the lane", 'C': "The 'wide' scope can read only lanes the scheduler can see, so it is merely redundant", 'D': "The 'wide' scope disables retry back-off for the tile"}
rationale: The 'wide' scope lets a tile read every lane, including underscore lanes, which is far broader than the two lanes needed.

stem: A snapshot of lane 'east' is taken while a 5 MB ferry from lane 'west' to 'east' is still in transit. At that moment, tile E2 in 'east' has already passed its gate. The snapshot is later restored. Which statement correctly describes the restored state?
options: {'A': 'Lane memory and the in-transit ferry data are both restored, and E2 continues past its gate', 'B': 'Lane memory is restored, the in-transit ferry data is not, and E2 must satisfy its gate again', 'C': 'Lane memory is restored, the ferry shards are restored in their original order, and E2 continues past its gate', 'D': 'Only the ferry data is restored, and E2 resumes exactly where it was'}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, and restoring re-runs gates from scratch.

stem: Lane 'intake' sent a batch of records to lane 'scoring' by ferry. A snapshot of 'scoring' was taken partway through the beat, and the lane was later restored from it. The 'scoring' lane memory looks correct, but the records from that batch are missing entirely. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The batch was over 2 MB and its shards arrived out of order', 'B': "'ledger.compact' was run and deleted the batch from lane memory", 'C': 'The batch was still in transit in the ferry when the snapshot was taken, so it was not captured', 'D': "The 'trace' flag was off, so the batch was never written to lane memory"}
rationale: Snapshots do not capture ferry contents in transit, so data still in the ferry at snapshot time is lost on restore.

stem: A tile produces an incorrect output intermittently, and the operator needs to inspect that output after a failure. Which approach will actually capture the output?
options: {'A': "Enable the 'trace' flag on the tile and read the trace after the next failure", 'B': "Read the lane's metrics, which record every tile event", 'C': 'Let the tile retry, because retries record the output of the previous attempt', 'D': 'Have the tile write its output to lane memory and take a snapshot of the lane'}
rationale: The 'trace' flag records inputs only and metrics are sampled only every 5th beat, but snapshots do capture lane memory.

stem: Metric sampling has been running since beat 1. A tile's memory usage spiked sharply during beat 7 and returned to normal by beat 9. The operator checks the metrics, but no spike appears. Which explanation is correct?
options: {'A': 'Metrics are sampled only on every 5th beat, so beat 7 fell between the samples at beats 5 and 10', 'B': "The 'trace' flag was off, and metrics are collected only for traced tiles", 'C': "'ledger.compact' was run, which removed the spike from metric history", 'D': 'Metrics record only tile inputs, never resource usage'}
rationale: Metrics are sampled on every 5th beat, and events between samples are not recorded.

stem: Lane '_audit' runs only because it is pinned, and the pin was renewed with 'pin.renew' two beats ago. The operator then upgrades Tessellate to a newer version. What happens to '_audit' after the upgrade?
options: {'A': 'It keeps running for the remaining 10 beats of the renewed pin', 'B': 'It keeps running indefinitely, because recently renewed pins survive upgrades', 'C': 'It stops running, because the upgrade resets all pins and underscore lanes run only when pinned', 'D': 'It keeps running, but its tile cap rises from 3 to 7'}
rationale: Upgrading resets all pins, and an underscore lane is invisible to the scheduler unless pinned, so '_audit' no longer runs.

stem: An operator copies a configuration from documentation for a newer Tessellate release. It contains 'retry.limit = 4' and a key, 'retry.jitter', that exists only in that newer release. The cluster runs the older version. The configuration loads with no errors or warnings, but retry timing shows no jitter. What is the cause?
options: {'A': "A 'retry.limit' above 3 disables retry back-off, which also disables jitter", 'B': "The running version does not recognise 'retry.jitter' and ignores it without warning", 'C': 'Retry settings apply only to tiles in pinned lanes', 'D': "Retries reuse the tile's original inputs, which overrides any timing settings"}
rationale: Configuration keys unknown to the running version are ignored without warning, and a 'retry.limit' of 4 does not exceed the threshold of 5 that disables back-off.

stem: Lane A has 3 tiles. Lane B has 4 tiles, and one of them sits idle for the whole run. A ferry with ferry.eager = true sends data from lane A to lane B. Both lanes run for 10 beats. What is the combined billing weight of the two lanes?
rationale: Lane A's weight is 3 × 10 = 30 (L1). An eager ferry doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane (F3), and idle tiles still count (L1). Lane B's weight is therefore 4 × 10 × 2 = 80, for a total of 110. 70 ignores the doubling. 90 drops the idle tile. 140 wrongly doubles the sending lane as well.

stem: A ferry carries ordered event batches from lane ingest to lane report. Batches of about 1 MB have arrived in correct order. One 6 MB batch reached the receiver with its events scrambled. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The beat was too short, so two ferry copies overlapped mid-transfer', 'B': 'The batch was split into shards that arrived and stayed out of order', 'C': 'Eager mode was on, which reorders data to cut latency at the receiver', 'D': 'The receiving lane was full, so tiles consumed the batch in parallel'}
rationale: Ferries larger than 2 MB are split into shards (F2). Shards can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them. The 1 MB batches were never sharded, which is why only the large batch was scrambled.

stem: An operator sets retry.limit = 6. A tile then fails because of bad upstream data, and the upstream data is corrected shortly afterwards. How will the tile's retries behave?
options: {'A': 'Up to 6 retries with back-off, each using the corrected upstream data', 'B': 'Up to 6 retries fire immediately, each using the corrected upstream data', 'C': 'Up to 6 retries with back-off, each using the original inputs', 'D': 'Up to 6 retries fire immediately, each using the original inputs'}
rationale: A retry.limit above 5 disables back-off, so retries fire immediately (R2). Retries also reuse the tile's original inputs even if upstream data has changed (R1).

stem: A tile failed because its upstream data was wrong. The upstream data has since been corrected, but each retry of the tile still fails the same way. Which action will get the tile to run on the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Cancel the tile and submit a new one that reads current upstream data', 'B': 'Raise retry.limit to 5 so later attempts can pick up the fixed data', 'C': 'Wait one beat so a ferry delivers the fix before the next retry runs', 'D': 'Take a snapshot now so the next retry restarts from fresh lane state'}
rationale: Retries reuse the tile's original inputs regardless of upstream changes (R1). More retries, waiting for a ferry, or taking a snapshot will not change those inputs. Only a newly submitted tile reads the current data.

stem: A reporting job consists of 5 independent tiles. All 5 must run on every beat for 30 consecutive beats. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'One pinned lane of 5 tiles, with pin.renew issued every 10 beats', 'B': 'Two pinned lanes of 3 and 2 tiles, with pin.renew issued every 10 beats', 'C': 'Two pinned lanes of 3 and 2 tiles, pinned once at the start of the run', 'D': 'One pinned lane of 5 tiles, pinned once at the start of the run'}
rationale: A pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles (P1), so 5 tiles need two pinned lanes. Pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed (P2), so renewing every 10 beats keeps both lanes guaranteed to run for all 30 beats.

stem: The lane nightly had been pinned and renewed regularly, and it ran on every beat. Immediately after Tessellate was upgraded from 4.1 to 4.2, nightly began being skipped on many beats. Its configuration was not changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': "The upgrade lowered the lane's tile cap, so all of its tiles were queued", 'B': "The upgrade changed the default beat length, so the lane's gates stay shut", 'C': "The upgrade cleared the lane's pin, so running on each beat is not guaranteed", 'D': 'The upgrade hid the lane from the scheduler until it is given a new name'}
rationale: Upgrading Tessellate resets all pins (V1). Without its pin, nightly is no longer guaranteed to run on every beat (P1).

stem: Two lanes each hold 3 tiles and run on every beat. The team wants to lower its billing weight without removing any tiles. Which change achieves this?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact after each beat to trim the stored history', 'B': 'Split each lane into smaller lanes so the tiles finish sooner', 'C': 'Pin both lanes so the scheduler runs them more efficiently', 'D': 'Combine both lanes into a single lane holding all six tiles'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes into one reduces billing weight (L2). ledger.compact does not reduce billing weight (L3). Splitting lanes never reduces it (L2). Pinning only guarantees runs and caps lanes at 3 tiles (P1).

stem: During a cost review, four engineers each state an assumption about Tessellate billing. Which assumption is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Running ledger.compact regularly will bring our billing weight down', 'B': 'Idle tiles in a running lane still add to our billing weight', 'C': "Turning on eager ferries into a lane will raise that lane's weight", 'D': 'Merging two half-full lanes into one will cut our billing weight'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight (L3). The other three statements are correct according to L1, F3 and L2.

stem: An unpinned lane already holds 7 tiles. An operator submits another tile to the same lane. What happens to the new tile?
options: {'A': 'It is rejected, and the submit command returns a capacity error', 'B': 'It waits in a queue, and no warning or error is reported', 'C': 'It is moved into an automatically created overflow lane', 'D': 'It replaces the oldest tile, which is returned to the queue'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles. An 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected (T1).

stem: Five tiles must exchange large intermediate state with each other many times within each beat. Four other tiles need only a summary of the results once per beat. No lanes will be pinned. Which layout meets these needs?
options: {'A': 'All nine tiles in one lane so every tile can use shared memory', 'B': 'The five tiles in lane _shared, the four in a lane fed by a ferry', 'C': 'The five tiles in one lane, the four in a second lane fed by a ferry', 'D': 'Each of the five tiles in its own lane, linked by eager ferries'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane share memory (T2), so the five tiles belong together. A once-per-beat ferry suits the summary (F1). Nine tiles exceed the 7-tile limit, so extra tiles would be queued (T1). An underscore lane never runs unless pinned (T3). Separate lanes can exchange data only once per beat by ferry, and eager mode doubles billing weight (F1, F3).

stem: A tile in lane `ingest` waits on a gate named `files_ready`. The engine uses the default beat, and a beat boundary has just passed. Ten seconds later, the `files_ready` condition becomes true. If nothing else intervenes, when does the tile proceed?
options: {'A': 'Within about a second of the condition becoming true', 'B': 'At the next beat, roughly 30 seconds after it became true', 'C': "When the tile's next scheduled retry attempt fires", 'D': 'When an operator triggers a manual gate re-check'}
rationale: Rule G1 says gates are checked once per beat, not continuously. With the default 40-second beat, a condition that becomes true 10 seconds after a check is seen at the next check, about 30 seconds later. Immediate unblocking is the usual intuition but is wrong here. Retries and manual re-checks do not control gate evaluation.

stem: Tile `publish` passed the gate `approval_signed` and was then captured in a snapshot. The approval was a one-time signal that has since been cleared. After the snapshot is restored, `publish` sits blocked at that gate. What best explains this?
options: {'A': "The snapshot left out lane memory, so the tile's inputs are missing", 'B': 'The restored lane lost its pin, and unpinned lanes skip gate checks', 'C': 'Restoring re-evaluated the gate from the start, and its condition is false', 'D': 'The snapshot stored the gate as blocked because it was taken mid-beat'}
rationale: Rule S2 says restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, so a tile that was past a gate can block again. Here the approval signal has been cleared, so the condition is now false and the tile blocks. Snapshots do capture lane memory (S1). Pins have no effect on whether gates are checked. Snapshots do not store a mid-beat gate state.

stem: Lane `reports` holds five tiles that all need the `wide` scope. A sixth tile, `export`, sits in the same lane and consumes output from one of those tiles. For compliance, `export` must be unable to read any other lane. Which configuration meets the requirement?
options: {'A': 'Move export to its own narrow-scope lane and feed it by a ferry', 'B': 'Give export a narrow tile-level scope and keep the lane at wide', 'C': 'Put export behind a gate that blocks reads from outside its lane', 'D': 'Pin the reports lane so its tiles run under a restricted scope'}
rationale: Rule G3 says permissions are inherited from the lane, and a tile cannot hold a narrower scope than its lane. A tile-level restriction inside a wide lane therefore cannot work. The tile has to live in a separate lane with a narrow scope, and it receives its input data through a ferry (T2). Gates block on conditions, not reads. Pinning changes scheduling and the tile cap, not scope.

stem: Lane `_audit` holds confidential records. An operator reviews four proposed changes. Which change would let a tile outside `_audit` read that lane's data?
options: {'A': 'Adding a ferry that carries status flags from `metrics` into `_audit`', 'B': 'Enabling the trace flag on every tile running in lane `metrics`', 'C': 'Pinning lane `metrics` so that it runs on every beat alongside `_audit`', 'D': 'Granting the dashboard tile in lane `metrics` the broadest read scope'}
rationale: Rule G2 says the `wide` scope (the broadest read scope) lets a tile read every lane, including underscore lanes. Being hidden from the scheduler does not protect `_audit` from a wide grant. A ferry into `_audit` moves data toward it, not out of it. Trace records the inputs of the `metrics` tiles only. Pinning affects scheduling, not read access.

stem:
A snapshot is taken while three things are true:
- Lane `stage` has intermediate results in memory.
- A 3 MB ferry from `stage` to lane `load` is mid-transit.
- A tile in `load` has already passed its gate.

What is the state immediately after this snapshot is restored?
options: {'A': 'Lane memory and the in-transit ferry data return; the load tile keeps its passed gate', 'B': 'Lane memory returns; the in-transit ferry data is gone; the load tile must pass its gate again', 'C': 'Lane memory and the in-transit ferry data return; the load tile must pass its gate again', 'D': 'Lane memory returns; the in-transit ferry data is gone; the load tile keeps its passed gate'}
rationale: Rule S1 says snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, so the ferry data is lost. Rule S2 says restoring re-runs gates from scratch, so the `load` tile must pass its gate again. Only option B combines both effects.

stem: Lane `fetch` sent a batch to lane `summarize` about 20 seconds before a snapshot was taken. The engine uses the default beat. After the snapshot is restored, `fetch` still has the batch in its memory, but `summarize` has no trace of it. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The snapshot was taken between two metric sampling beats', 'B': 'The batch exceeded 2 MB and its shards arrived out of order', 'C': 'The batch was still being ferried when the snapshot was taken', 'D': 'The summarize lane held more than seven tiles at snapshot time'}
rationale: Ferries copy data once per 40-second beat (F1), so a batch sent 20 seconds earlier was probably still in transit. Rule S1 says in-transit ferry contents are not captured by snapshots. Metric sampling does not affect snapshots. Out-of-order shards still arrive. An 8th tile is queued, which does not erase data.

stem: Tile `render` intermittently produces a malformed result before failing. An operator needs a copy of the exact result it produced so it can be inspected later. Which approach captures that result?
options: {'A': 'Enable the trace flag on render and read what it records', 'B': "Read render's results from the metrics dashboard afterwards", 'C': "Raise retry.limit so that each failed attempt's result is kept", 'D': 'Have render write to lane memory, then snapshot the lane'}
rationale: Rule O1 says trace records tile inputs only, never outputs, so it cannot capture the result. Snapshots capture lane memory (S1), so writing the result to lane memory and taking a snapshot preserves it. Metrics are sampled every 5th beat (O2) and do not hold outputs. Raising retry.limit changes back-off behaviour, not retention.

stem: Tile `merge` in the ordinary lane `etl` had a severe memory spike that lasted a single beat. An operator checks the metrics afterwards and finds no sign of it. No one has changed any configuration or run any commands. Why is the spike missing?
options: {'A': 'Metrics are collected periodically, and the spike fell between collections', 'B': 'Lane etl was unpinned, and metrics from unpinned lanes are dropped', 'C': 'The trace flag was off for merge, so its runtime events went unrecorded', 'D': 'ledger.compact trimmed history, removing the data for that beat'}
rationale: Rule O2 says metrics are sampled on every 5th beat, and events between samples are not recorded, so a one-beat spike can be missed. Pinning has no effect on metrics. Trace records inputs, not metrics (O1). The stem rules out ledger.compact, because no commands were run.

stem: Lane `billing` is pinned, and its pin was renewed with `pin.renew` two beats ago. The operator then upgrades Tessellate to a newer release. What is billing's status right after the upgrade?
options: {'A': 'Still pinned until the remainder of its 12-beat term runs out', 'B': 'Still pinned, with a fresh 12-beat term starting at the upgrade', 'C': 'No longer pinned, and scheduled the same as any ordinary lane', 'D': 'Still pinned, but with its tile cap raised from 3 tiles to 7'}
rationale: Rule V1 says upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, regardless of how recently they were renewed. The billing lane therefore becomes an ordinary unpinned lane.

stem: An operator copies a working configuration file from the staging cluster to the production cluster. Both clusters start cleanly and log no warnings. The setting `shard.reorder = true` has a visible effect in staging but none in production, even though production sends ferries larger than 2 MB. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': "Production's lanes are pinned, and pinned lanes override ferry settings", 'B': 'Production runs a release that does not know this key, so it is dropped', 'C': 'The setting takes effect in production after the next pin renewal', 'D': 'Production uses eager ferries, which bypass shard-handling settings'}
rationale: Rule V2 says configuration keys unknown to the running version are ignored without warning. That fits a clean start with no effect, which points to production running a different release that lacks the key. No rule ties ferry or shard settings to pins or pin renewal. Eager ferries affect latency and billing (F3), not shard handling.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets ferry.eager = true on a ferry that carries a 5 MB payload from lane Alpha to lane Beta. Lane Beta has 4 tiles and runs for 10 beats. Which outcome should the operator expect?
options: {'A': "Latency drops, the payload arrives as one ordered block, and Beta's billing weight is 40.", 'B': "Latency drops, the payload is split into shards that Tessellate reorders on arrival, and Beta's billing weight is 80.", 'C': "Latency drops, the payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order, and Beta's billing weight is 80.", 'D': "Latency drops, the payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order, and Alpha's billing weight doubles instead of Beta's."}
rationale: Ferries over 2 MB are split into shards that are not reordered, and eager mode doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane, which takes Beta from 4 × 10 = 40 to 80.

stem: A team ferries records from lane Ingest to lane Report. Small batches always arrive in the correct order. Batches larger than 2 MB sometimes arrive with records scrambled, but no records are missing. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'Large ferries are split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not put the shards back in order.', 'B': 'The ferry beat is too short, so Tessellate interleaves records from consecutive beats.', 'C': 'Retries in the Ingest lane reuse old inputs, which inserts stale records in the middle of the batch.', 'D': 'The Report lane exceeded 7 tiles, so some tiles were queued and read their data late.'}
rationale: Ferries larger than 2 MB are sharded, the shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them, which matches a problem that appears only with large batches.

stem: An operator sets retry.limit = 6 on a tile. The tile fails, and while it is retrying, an upstream lane publishes corrected input data. How will the retries behave?
options: {'A': 'The retries use increasing back-off delays and pick up the corrected input data.', 'B': 'The retries fire immediately and pick up the corrected input data.', 'C': 'The retries use increasing back-off delays and reuse the original input data.', 'D': 'The retries fire immediately with no back-off and reuse the original input data.'}
rationale: Raising retry.limit above 5 disables back-off so retries fire immediately, and retries always reuse the tile's original inputs even if upstream data has changed.

stem: A tile failed because an upstream lane produced bad data. The upstream data has since been fixed, but every retry of the tile keeps failing in the same way. Which action will most directly get the tile to run on the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit above 5 so the tile gets more retry attempts.', 'B': 'Stop relying on the retries and launch a new run of the tile so that it reads the current upstream data.', 'C': 'Turn on the trace flag so the retries record their outputs.', 'D': "Run ledger.compact to clear the tile's stored history before the next retry."}
rationale: Retries always reuse the tile's original inputs, so only a newly started tile will read the corrected upstream data.

stem: A job must run on every single beat for 30 beats. Its work needs 5 independent tiles. No Tessellate upgrade is planned during the job. Which setup meets the requirement?
options: {'A': 'Put all 5 tiles in one lane, pin it once, and leave it for the 30 beats.', 'B': 'Put all 5 tiles in one unpinned lane, because unpinned lanes hold up to 7 tiles and run on every beat.', 'C': 'Split the tiles into two pinned lanes of 3 and 2 tiles, and run pin.renew on both lanes before their pins reach 12 beats.', 'D': 'Split the tiles into two pinned lanes of 3 and 2 tiles, pin them once, and rely on the pins lasting for the whole job.'}
rationale: A pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles and its pin expires after 12 beats, so the 5 tiles need two pinned lanes whose pins are renewed during the 30-beat job.

stem: A lane named _nightly was pinned and ran on every beat. After exactly 12 beats it stopped running. No tile failed, no errors were logged, and Tessellate was not upgraded. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': 'The lane went over its tile limit, so all new tiles were silently queued.', 'B': 'The pin expired after 12 beats without being renewed, and a lane whose name starts with an underscore does not run unless it is pinned.', 'C': 'A tile failure in the pinned lane failed the whole run.', 'D': 'The pin was reset by a version change, which always happens after 12 beats.'}
rationale: Pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed with pin.renew, and lanes with a leading underscore never run unless pinned, so the lane stops without any error.

stem: Two lanes each hold 3 tiles, and both lanes run on every beat. In each lane only one tile does useful work, and the other two sit idle. Which change will reduce the total billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact on both lanes.', 'B': 'Split each lane into three lanes of one tile each.', 'C': 'Mark the idle tiles as idle so that they stop counting toward billing while their lanes keep running.', 'D': 'Merge the two half-full lanes into a single lane.'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes into one lane reduces billing weight, whereas compaction does not, splitting lanes never does, and idle tiles in a running lane still count.

stem: During a cost review, a teammate makes four claims about Tessellate billing. Which claim is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Running ledger.compact will lower our billing weight because it removes stored history.', 'B': 'Idle tiles in a lane that is running still add to billing weight.', 'C': 'Turning on ferry.eager will double the billing weight of the tiles in the receiving lane.', 'D': 'A lane with 4 tiles that runs for 10 beats has a billing weight of 40.'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight, so this claim is wrong while the other three match the billing rules.

stem: An unpinned lane already holds 7 tiles. An operator submits an 8th tile to the same lane. What happens?
options: {'A': 'Tessellate rejects the 8th tile with a capacity error.', 'B': 'Tessellate automatically creates a second lane and places the 8th tile there.', 'C': 'The 8th tile is silently queued, and no error or warning is shown.', 'D': 'Tessellate evicts the oldest tile to make room for the 8th tile.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, and an 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: Three tiles must continuously share a working dataset of several megabytes. They need low latency and must see the records in a consistent order. Each tile only needs to run on beats when it has work. Which layout fits best?
options: {'A': 'Put each tile in its own lane and connect the lanes with ferries set to ferry.eager = true.', 'B': 'Put all three tiles in the same ordinary lane so that they share memory directly.', 'C': 'Put each tile in its own lane and connect the lanes with default ferries.', 'D': 'Put all three tiles in a lane named _shared to isolate them from the scheduler.'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane share memory, which avoids ferry beat latency, the out-of-order shards on transfers over 2 MB, and the doubled eager billing, while an underscore lane would never run unless pinned.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile waits behind a gate, and the lane uses the default beat length. The gate is checked at t = 0 seconds, and its condition is false at that moment. The condition becomes true at t = 5 seconds and stays true. At about what time can the tile proceed?
options: {'A': 'At about t = 5 seconds, as soon as the condition becomes true.', 'B': 'At about t = 40 seconds, when the gate is next checked.', 'C': 'At about t = 200 seconds, on the next 5th-beat check.', 'D': 'Never, until the run is restarted, because gates are checked only once when a tile starts.'}
rationale: Gates are checked once per beat rather than continuously, and the default beat is 40 seconds, so the tile is released at the next check, around t = 40 seconds.

stem: A tile's gate waits for the flag `approved` to be true. The tile passed this gate, and the flag was then cleared as part of normal cleanup. Later, an operator restores a snapshot taken after the tile had passed the gate. The tile is now blocked at the same gate. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The snapshot did not capture lane memory, so the tile lost its record of having passed the gate.', 'B': "Ferry shards arrived out of order during the restore, which corrupted the gate's condition.", 'C': 'Restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, and the `approved` flag is now false, so the tile blocks again.', 'D': 'The restore reset all pins, which re-locked every gate in the lane.'}
rationale: Restoring a snapshot re-evaluates gates from scratch, so a tile that was already past a gate must satisfy the condition again, and the condition is now false.

stem: The lane `ingest` has the `wide` scope because one of its tiles must read every lane. A security review now requires that a second tile, `parser`, be able to read only data from its own lane. What change meets this least-access requirement?
options: {'A': 'Move `parser` into a separate lane that has a narrow scope, and pass it any data it needs from `ingest` through a ferry.', 'B': 'Give `parser` a narrower scope than `ingest` while keeping it in the `ingest` lane.', 'C': 'Rename the `ingest` lane to `_ingest` so that `parser` is hidden from other lanes.', 'D': 'Keep `parser` in `ingest` and turn off the `trace` flag so that its reads are not recorded.'}
rationale: Permissions are inherited from the lane and a tile cannot hold a narrower scope than its lane, so the tile must move to a narrower-scoped lane, and cross-lane data can only arrive by ferry.

stem: A tile needs to read only the lanes `orders` and `billing`. To save time, an operator grants it the `wide` scope. The system also has a hidden lane named `_audit`. What is the problem with this grant?
options: {'A': 'There is no problem, because `wide` covers visible lanes only and underscore lanes stay hidden from it.', 'B': "The `wide` scope doubles the billing weight of every tile in the tile's lane.", 'C': "The `wide` scope is ignored, because a tile's scope always comes from the tile itself, not from its lane.", 'D': 'The `wide` scope lets the tile read every lane, including the hidden `_audit` lane, which is far more access than it needs.'}
rationale: The `wide` scope grants read access to every lane, including underscore lanes such as `_audit`, so it is much broader than the two lanes required.

stem: An operator takes a snapshot of lane `alpha`. At that moment, `alpha`'s memory holds a batch X, a ferry is carrying batch Y from `alpha` to lane `beta`, and one tile in `alpha` has already passed its gate. The operator later restores this snapshot. Which statement describes the result?
options: {'A': 'Batch X and batch Y are both restored, and the tile stays past its gate.', 'B': 'Batch X is restored and the tile stays past its gate, but batch Y is lost.', 'C': 'Batch X is restored but batch Y is not, and the tile must pass its gate again.', 'D': 'Only batch Y is restored, because snapshots capture ferry contents rather than lane memory.'}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, and a restore re-runs gates from scratch, so the gated tile can block again.

stem: Lane `enrich` receives records from lane `ingest` by ferry. After a snapshot of both lanes is restored, `enrich` is missing a group of records. Logs show that these records were in a ferry between the two lanes when the snapshot was taken. Why were they lost?
options: {'A': 'Snapshots do not capture ferry contents in transit, so those records were not part of the restored state.', 'B': 'The ferry was larger than 2 MB, and Tessellate deletes shards that arrive out of order.', 'C': "Retries reuse a tile's original inputs, so the restored tiles discarded the newer records.", 'D': 'Running `ledger.compact` after the snapshot removed the records from the lanes.'}
rationale: A snapshot captures lane memory but not data in transit on a ferry, so records that were mid-ferry are absent after the restore.

stem: A tile intermittently produces wrong results, and an engineer needs to capture what the tile actually outputs on a failing run. Which approach will capture that output?
options: {'A': 'Turn on the `trace` flag for the tile.', 'B': "Read the tile's output from the metrics dashboard.", 'C': 'Raise `retry.limit` to 6 so that the failure repeats immediately and is easier to observe.', 'D': "Have the tile write its output into its lane's memory, then take a snapshot of the lane."}
rationale: The `trace` flag records only inputs and metrics are only sampled, but snapshots capture lane memory, so output written to lane memory will be preserved.

stem: Metrics are being collected from the start of a run. A lane's tile count spiked sharply during beats 6 through 9 and was back to normal by beat 10. The metrics dashboard shows no spike at all. What is the best explanation?
options: {'A': 'The `trace` flag was off, so the metrics system had no tile data to report.', 'B': 'Metrics are sampled only on every 5th beat, so samples were taken at beats 5 and 10 and the spike between them was not recorded.', 'C': 'Idle tiles do not count toward metrics, so the spike was filtered out.', 'D': 'Metrics are recorded continuously, but a gate delayed them until after the spike had ended.'}
rationale: Metrics are sampled on every 5th beat and events between samples are not recorded, so a spike confined to beats 6 through 9 falls between the samples at beats 5 and 10.

stem: Before an upgrade, the lanes `reports` and `_audit` are both pinned, and each pin was renewed two beats ago. The operator then upgrades Tessellate. What happens immediately after the upgrade?
options: {'A': 'Both pins are reset, so `reports` is no longer guaranteed to run on every beat and `_audit` stops running until it is pinned again.', 'B': 'Both pins stay active until they reach their normal 12-beat expiry.', 'C': 'Both pins are renewed automatically as part of the upgrade.', 'D': 'The upgrade is refused until both pins are removed manually.'}
rationale: Upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, and an underscore lane never runs unless it is pinned.

stem: An operator adds `pin.autorenew = true` to the configuration of a Tessellate installation. This key was introduced in a newer version than the one the installation runs. In the same change, the operator also raises `retry.limit` to 6. No errors or warnings appear, yet the pinned lane loses its pin after 12 beats. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The `pin.autorenew` setting applies only to underscore lanes, so it had no effect on this lane.', 'B': 'The pinned lane held more than 3 tiles, so the pin was cancelled.', 'C': 'The running version does not recognise `pin.autorenew` and ignores it without warning, so the pin expired normally after 12 beats.', 'D': 'Raising `retry.limit` above 5 turned off back-off, and that cancels all pins.'}
rationale: Configuration keys unknown to the running version are ignored silently, so the pin followed its normal 12-beat expiry with no automatic renewal.

stem: An operator configures a ferry from lane `ingest` to lane `scoring`. Each beat the ferry carries a 5 MB payload. `ferry.eager = true` is set. `scoring` holds 6 tiles, 2 of which are usually idle. The lanes run for 10 beats. What should the operator expect?
options: {'A': 'The payload arrives in the order it was sent because eager ferries bypass sharding. Billing weight for `scoring` is 60.', 'B': 'The payload is split into shards that Tessellate reorders on arrival. Billing weight for `scoring` is 120.', 'C': 'The payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order and are not reordered. Billing weight for `scoring` is 120.', 'D': 'The payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order. Billing weight for `scoring` is 80, because only the 4 busy tiles are doubled.'}
rationale: F2: a ferry over 2 MB is split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them. F3: eager mode doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane. L1: idle tiles still count. So the weight is 6 tiles × 10 beats × 2 = 120.

stem: A pipeline ferries time-series records from one lane to another. Small daily batches always arrive in the correct order. Since batches grew to about 3 MB, the receiving tile intermittently processes records out of sequence. Nothing else changed. What is the most likely cause, and what is the appropriate remedy?
options: {'A': 'Ferries over 2 MB are split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them. Embed sequence numbers in the records and sort on receipt.', 'B': 'The ferry is running in eager mode, which drops ordering guarantees. Set `ferry.eager = false` and Tessellate will restore order.', 'C': 'The beat is too short for large payloads. Lengthen the beat so the ferry has time to deliver the records in order.', 'D': "The receiving tile's retries reuse old inputs. Lower `retry.limit` so stale out-of-order records are not replayed."}
rationale: F2: payloads over 2 MB are sharded, shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate never reorders them. Order-sensitive data must therefore carry its own sequence numbers. The eager setting, beat length, and retry settings do not affect shard ordering.

stem: A tile in an unpinned lane reads a corrupted upstream file and fails. The operator has set `retry.limit = 6`. Within seconds of the failure, an upstream team replaces the file with a corrected version. What happens next?
options: {'A': 'Retries back off exponentially, and later retries pick up the corrected file and succeed. The run continues normally.', 'B': 'Retries fire immediately with no back-off and read the corrected file. Only the first retry might fail.', 'C': 'Retries back off normally but keep using the original corrupted inputs. Once they are exhausted, the whole run fails.', 'D': 'Retries fire immediately with no back-off and keep using the original corrupted inputs. Once they are exhausted, only that lane fails.'}
rationale: R2: a `retry.limit` above 5 disables back-off, so retries fire immediately. R1: retries reuse the tile's original inputs even if upstream data changed. R3: a failure in an unpinned lane fails only that lane, not the whole run.

stem: A tile failed because an upstream lane produced bad data. The upstream data has now been fixed, but every retry still fails with the same error. Which action will actually let the tile process the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Raise `retry.limit` to 10 so the tile gets enough attempts to see the fix.', 'B': 'Let the retries finish, then start a new tile run so it reads the current upstream data.', 'C': 'Switch the incoming ferry to `ferry.eager = true` so the fixed data reaches the retrying tile sooner.', 'D': 'Take a snapshot of the lane and restore it so the retry re-reads its inputs.'}
rationale: R1: retries always reuse the original inputs, so no retry setting or faster ferry will make a retry see fixed upstream data. Option A also disables back-off (R2). Option C only affects delivery to new work and doubles billing (F3). Snapshots capture lane memory and do not change retry semantics (S1, S2). A fresh tile run reads the current inputs.

stem: A compliance job consists of 5 independent tiles, which share no memory. Every tile must run on every beat for 30 consecutive beats. No Tessellate upgrade is scheduled. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Put all 5 tiles in one pinned lane and pin it once at the start.', 'B': 'Put all 5 tiles in one pinned lane and run `pin.renew` every 10 beats.', 'C': 'Split the tiles into two pinned lanes of 3 and 2 tiles, and run `pin.renew` on each lane before 12 beats elapse, repeating as needed.', 'D': 'Put all 5 tiles in an unpinned lane named `_compliance` so the scheduler gives it reserved capacity.'}
rationale: P1: a pinned lane runs on every beat but is capped at 3 tiles, so 5 tiles need two pinned lanes. P2: pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed, so a 30-beat job requires renewal. Options A and B exceed the 3-tile cap, and A also lets the pin expire. T3: an underscore lane that is not pinned never runs.

stem: Lane `_audit` was pinned at beat 1 and ran correctly on every beat. Starting at beat 13, it stopped running entirely. The lane has 2 tiles, no gates, and no failures, and Tessellate was not upgraded. What explains this?
options: {'A': 'The lane exceeded its tile capacity, so new tiles were queued behind the existing ones.', 'B': 'Metrics are sampled only every 5th beat, so the lane is still running but appears idle.', 'C': 'A tile failure in the pinned lane failed the whole run at beat 12.', 'D': 'The pin expired after 12 beats without `pin.renew`. Because underscore lanes never run unless pinned, the lane stopped.'}
rationale: P2: pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed. T3: a lane with a leading underscore is invisible to the scheduler and never runs unless pinned. With 2 tiles the lane is under every cap (T1, P1), and the stem rules out failures. The lane genuinely stopped from beat 13, so the metrics-sampling explanation does not fit.

stem: Lanes `alpha` and `beta` each hold 3 tiles (half of a 7-tile lane would be 3.5) and run every beat. A ferry connects them. The team wants to lower billing weight without dropping any work. Which change does this?
options: {'A': 'Run `ledger.compact` every night to shrink the accumulated ledger.', 'B': 'Merge `alpha` and `beta` into a single lane of 6 tiles, which also removes the need for the ferry.', 'C': 'Split each lane into smaller lanes of 1–2 tiles so idle capacity is spread out.', 'D': 'Set `ferry.eager = true` on the ferry into `beta` so work finishes with less waiting.'}
rationale: L2: merging two half-full lanes reduces billing weight, and splitting lanes never does. L3: `ledger.compact` reduces stored history but not billing weight. F3: eager mode doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane.

stem: During a cost review, four engineers state assumptions. Which assumption is mistaken?
options: {'A': '"Our ledger is huge. If we run `ledger.compact`, next month\'s billing weight will drop."', 'B': '"The idle tiles in our running lanes are still adding to billing weight."', 'C': '"Turning on eager ferries into `reports` will double the billing weight of every tile in that lane."', 'D': '"Combining our two half-empty lanes into one should cut billing weight."'}
rationale: L3: `ledger.compact` reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight. The other statements are correct: idle tiles count (L1), eager ferries double the receiving lane's weight (F3), and merging half-full lanes reduces weight (L2).

stem: A lane currently holds 7 tiles. An operator submits an 8th tile to the same lane. No errors appear in the console. What happened to the 8th tile?
options: {'A': 'It was rejected, and the error was suppressed because the lane is full.', 'B': 'Tessellate automatically created a sibling lane and placed the tile there.', 'C': 'It was silently queued in that lane and will wait rather than run alongside the other 7.', 'D': 'It replaced the oldest tile in the lane, which was evicted.'}
rationale: T1: a lane holds at most 7 tiles, and an 8th tile is silently queued, not rejected. Tessellate neither auto-creates lanes nor evicts tiles.

stem: Four tiles must exchange a 10 MB mutable working set many times per beat. The order of updates matters. The tiles do not need guaranteed every-beat scheduling. Which layout is correct?
options: {'A': 'Place each tile in its own lane and connect the lanes with eager ferries for low latency.', 'B': 'Place all four tiles in one pinned lane so they share memory and are guaranteed to run.', 'C': 'Place all four tiles in an unpinned lane named `_shared` to keep the working set private.', 'D': 'Place all four tiles in one ordinary unpinned lane so they share memory directly.'}
rationale: T2: tiles in the same lane share memory, while different lanes can exchange data only via ferries. Ferries copy once per beat (F1), and 10 MB payloads are sharded and may arrive out of order (F2). Eager ferries also double billing (F3). A pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles (P1), so one tile would not fit. An unpinned underscore lane never runs (T3).

stem: A Tessellate lane runs on the default beat. A tile is waiting on a gate whose condition becomes true 5 seconds after the most recent gate check. When will the tile be released?
options: {'A': 'Immediately, within a second of the condition becoming true', 'B': "After 5 more beats, when the gate's condition has been confirmed stable", 'C': 'At the next once-per-beat gate check, about 35 seconds later', 'D': 'Never, until the tile is retried with fresh inputs'}
rationale: Gates are checked once per beat, not continuously (G1). The default beat is 40 seconds (F1). The condition became true 5 seconds after a check, so the tile waits about 35 seconds for the next check. Gates do not need repeated confirmation, and retries are unrelated to gates.

stem: Before a snapshot was taken, tile `merge-3` had already passed its gate `upstream_ready` and was processing. The operator restores that snapshot. `merge-3` is now blocked on `upstream_ready` again, even though lane memory shows the data it was processing. What explains this?
options: {'A': 'Restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, and `upstream_ready` is not currently true', 'B': 'Snapshots do not capture lane memory, so the tile has lost its place and is waiting for data', 'C': "The restore reset the lane's pin, and unpinned lanes ignore gates until re-pinned", 'D': 'The tile is in its retry phase, and retries always re-block on the original gate with the original inputs'}
rationale: Restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, so tiles that were past a gate may block again (S2). Snapshots do capture lane memory (S1), so B is wrong. Pins are reset by upgrades, not restores (V1). Retries reuse original inputs but have nothing to do with gate re-evaluation.

stem: Lane `reports` has the `wide` scope because its existing tiles must read several lanes, including `_audit`. You must add a new tile that uses data produced by `reports` tiles but must NOT be able to read `_audit`. Which approach meets this least-access requirement?
options: {'A': 'Add the tile to `reports` and assign the tile itself a narrow scope that excludes `_audit`', 'B': 'Add the tile to `reports` and rename `_audit` to `audit` so the `wide` scope no longer applies to it', 'C': 'Add the tile to `reports` and pin the lane, because pinned lanes cap tile permissions to the default scope', 'D': 'Place the tile in a separate lane without the `wide` scope and deliver the data it needs from `reports` via a ferry'}
rationale: Permissions are inherited from the lane, and a tile cannot hold a narrower scope than its lane (G3). Any tile in `reports` therefore gets `wide` and can read every lane, including underscore lanes (G2). Data crosses lanes only through a ferry (T2), so the tile goes in a narrower lane and receives data by ferry. Renaming `_audit` would not remove access, because `wide` reads every lane. Renaming would also make the lane visible to the scheduler (T3). Pinning does not change scope.

stem: One tile in lane `billing` needs to read lane `metrics`. To allow this, an operator granted the `wide` scope to the `billing` lane. Lane `billing` contains six tiles. What is the problem with this grant?
options: {'A': 'There is no problem: `wide` excludes underscore lanes, so only normal lanes like `metrics` become readable', 'B': 'Every tile in `billing` can now read every lane, including underscore lanes such as `_audit`', 'C': 'Only the one requesting tile receives `wide`, but it can now also write to `metrics`', 'D': '`wide` causes underscore lanes to become visible to the scheduler, so `_audit` will start running'}
rationale: `wide` lets a tile read every lane, including underscore lanes (G2). Permissions are inherited from the lane, so all six tiles get the scope, not just one (G3). The grant does not exclude underscore lanes. It also does not make them run; only pinning does that (T3).

stem: A snapshot is taken while a ferry is carrying a batch from lane `ingest` to lane `score`. At that moment some tiles in `score` have already passed gate `batch_seen`. Later the snapshot is restored. Which outcome should you expect?
options: {'A': "Both lanes' memory and the in-flight batch are restored, and the `score` tiles resume past their gate", 'B': 'The in-flight batch is restored, but lane memory is not, so both lanes start empty except for the batch', 'C': "Both lanes' memory is restored, the in-flight batch is absent, and the `score` tiles must pass `batch_seen` again", 'D': "Both lanes' memory is restored, the in-flight batch is absent, and the `score` tiles resume past their gate"}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit (S1). Restoring re-runs gates from scratch, so tiles that were past `batch_seen` must re-check it (S2). Only C reflects both rules.

stem: After restoring last night's snapshot, an operator finds that a group of records is missing. They existed in neither the source lane nor the destination lane after the restore. Logs show those records were being ferried between the two lanes at the exact moment the snapshot was taken. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The ferry exceeded 2 MB, and shards that arrive out of order are discarded during restore', 'B': '`ledger.compact` was run after the snapshot, which deleted the records from stored history', 'C': 'Snapshots capture only pinned lanes, and neither lane was pinned', 'D': 'Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, so the in-flight records were not saved'}
rationale: S1 states that snapshots do not capture ferry contents in transit. The records had left the source lane but not reached the destination, so neither restored lane holds them. Out-of-order shards are not discarded, only left unordered (F2). `ledger.compact` affects stored history, not snapshot contents. Snapshots are not limited to pinned lanes.

stem: A tile intermittently produces a malformed result, and you need to inspect the actual output it produced on a failing run. Which approach will capture that output?
options: {'A': 'Have the tile write its result into lane memory, then take a snapshot of the lane', 'B': 'Enable the `trace` flag on the tile and read the recorded trace after the failure', 'C': "Read the output from the lane's metrics, which record each tile's results", 'D': "Raise `retry.limit` above 5 so failing runs repeat immediately and the trace records each attempt's output"}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory (S1), so writing the result to lane memory and snapshotting preserves it. `trace` records inputs only, never outputs (O1). Metrics are sampled only every 5th beat and are not per-tile outputs (O2). A high retry limit just removes back-off (R2), and trace still would not record outputs.

stem: During beat 12 only, a lane's tile count spiked and then returned to normal. The metrics dashboard shows normal values for beats 10 and 15 and has no record of the spike. Nothing is misconfigured. Why is the spike missing?
options: {'A': 'The lane was not pinned, and metrics are recorded only for pinned lanes', 'B': 'Metrics are sampled on every 5th beat, so an event confined to beat 12 falls between samples and is not recorded', 'C': '`ledger.compact` was run, which removes metric history along with billing history', 'D': 'The `trace` flag was off, and metrics depend on trace data to record tile counts'}
rationale: Metrics are sampled on every 5th beat, and events between samples are not recorded (O2). Beats 10 and 15 were sampled; beat 12 was not. Metrics do not depend on pinning or trace. `ledger.compact` affects stored history, not metric sampling.

stem: Lane `_audit` has been pinned and was renewed with `pin.renew` two beats ago. The cluster is now upgraded to a newer Tessellate 4 release. Assuming no other action is taken, what happens to `_audit`?
options: {'A': 'It keeps running, because a pin renewed within the last 12 beats survives upgrades', 'B': 'It keeps running for 10 more beats, then stops when the renewed pin reaches its 12-beat expiry', 'C': 'It keeps running, but its tile cap rises from 3 to 7 because the upgrade clears pin limits', 'D': 'It stops running, because the upgrade resets all pins and underscore lanes run only when pinned'}
rationale: Upgrading resets all pins, regardless of recent renewal (V1). An underscore lane is invisible to the scheduler and never runs unless pinned (T3), so `_audit` stops immediately. The 12-beat expiry (P2) is irrelevant because the pin is already gone. A lane that does not run has no tile cap that matters.

stem: An operator on Tessellate 4 copied `ferry.reorder = true` from a preview document for a future version. The goal was to fix a large ferry whose shards arrive out of order. After deployment, no error or warning appeared, but the shards still arrive out of order. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': '`ferry.reorder` applies only to ferries under 2 MB, and this ferry is larger, so it is split anyway', 'B': '`ferry.reorder` takes effect only when `ferry.eager = true` is also set', 'C': 'The running version does not recognize `ferry.reorder` and ignores it without warning; Tessellate 4 never reorders shards', 'D': 'The setting takes effect only after the next pin renewal cycle of 12 beats'}
rationale: Configuration keys unknown to the running version are ignored without warning (V2). In Tessellate 4, ferries over 2 MB are sharded and never reordered (F2). Order-sensitive data must carry its own sequence numbers. The other options invent dependencies on ferry size, eager mode, or pin cycles that the reference does not support.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets ferry.eager = true on a ferry that carries a 3 MB payload from lane Alpha to lane Beta every beat. Which statement correctly describes the result?
options: {'A': 'Latency drops, Tessellate reassembles the shards in their original order, and the tiles in lane Alpha are billed at double weight.', 'B': 'Latency drops, the payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order and are not reordered, and every tile in lane Beta is billed at double weight.', 'C': 'The ferry is rejected, because eager ferries cannot carry payloads larger than 2 MB.', 'D': 'Latency drops, the payload arrives whole because eager ferries skip sharding, and every tile in lane Beta is billed at double weight.'}
rationale: Payloads over 2 MB are split into shards that Tessellate never reorders, and an eager ferry doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane, which here is Beta.

stem: A Tessellate 4 ferry moves customer records between two lanes. When a payload is about 1.5 MB, the records always arrive in order. When a payload is about 5 MB, the records sometimes arrive scrambled. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The beat is too long, so records from two beats are mixed together.', 'B': 'ferry.eager is not enabled, and only eager ferries preserve ordering.', 'C': 'Payloads over 2 MB are split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them.', 'D': 'The trace flag is enabled, and tracing rewrites the order of ferry outputs.'}
rationale: Ferries larger than 2 MB are sharded, the shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not put them back in order, so only the large payloads arrive scrambled.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile is configured with retry.limit = 6. The tile fails, and a few seconds later an upstream lane corrects the data that the tile had read. How will the tile's retries behave?
options: {'A': 'Up to 6 retries with increasing back-off, and each retry reads the corrected upstream data.', 'B': 'Up to 6 retries that fire immediately with no back-off, and each retry reads the corrected upstream data.', 'C': "Up to 6 retries that fire immediately with no back-off, and each retry reuses the tile's original inputs.", 'D': 'The limit is capped at 5, and those retries use normal back-off with the original inputs.'}
rationale: A retry.limit above 5 disables back-off so retries fire immediately, and retries always reuse the tile's original inputs even if upstream data has changed.

stem: A Tessellate 4 tile failed because an upstream value was wrong. The upstream team has since fixed the value, but every retry of the tile still fails with the old value. Which action will get the tile to process the corrected value?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit to 10 so the tile has more attempts to pick up the fix.', 'B': 'Lengthen the retry back-off so the retries happen after the fix has propagated.', 'C': 'Enable the trace flag on the tile so its inputs are refreshed before the next retry.', 'D': "Submit a fresh tile or a new run, because retries always reuse the tile's original inputs."}
rationale: Retries reuse the original inputs no matter what changes upstream, so only a new tile or run will read the corrected value; more retries or more time will not help.

stem: A Tessellate 4 lane called ingest contains 3 tiles. It must run on every single beat for the next 30 beats. A Tessellate version upgrade is scheduled about halfway through that period. Which setup meets the requirement?
options: {'A': 'Pin the lane once at the start, since a pin lasts until it is manually removed.', 'B': 'Pin the lane, renew the pin with pin.renew before every 12 beats pass, and re-pin it immediately after the upgrade.', 'C': 'Pin the lane once at the start and rely on the upgrade to refresh the pin halfway through.', 'D': 'Rename the lane to _ingest so the scheduler gives it priority on every beat.'}
rationale: A pin guarantees a run on every beat but expires after 12 beats unless renewed, and upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, so the pin must be renewed and also re-applied after the upgrade.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane named _reports was pinned and ran on every beat for exactly 12 beats. After that it stopped running. No errors were logged, and the rest of the run kept going normally. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': 'The lane exceeded 7 tiles, and the extra tiles blocked the whole lane.', 'B': 'The pin expired after 12 beats, and a lane whose name starts with an underscore never runs unless it is pinned.', 'C': 'A tile failed inside the pinned lane, and that failure stopped only this lane.', 'D': 'Metrics are sampled only on every 5th beat, so the lane is still running but looks idle.'}
rationale: Pins expire after 12 beats without pin.renew, and underscore lanes are invisible to the scheduler unless pinned, so the lane silently stopped.

stem: A Tessellate 4 workload uses two lanes. Each lane holds 3 tiles, and some of those tiles sit idle for most beats. Both lanes run for 20 beats. Which change will reduce the billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact after each run to shrink the ledger.', 'B': 'Split each lane into two smaller lanes so that each lane finishes sooner.', 'C': 'Merge the two half-full lanes into a single lane.', 'D': 'Leave the setup unchanged, because idle tiles are not counted toward billing weight.'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes into one lane reduces billing weight, whereas ledger.compact does not reduce it, splitting lanes never does, and idle tiles still count.

stem: A team lists four assumptions about Tessellate 4 costs. Which assumption is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles in a running lane still add to billing weight.', 'B': 'Running ledger.compact regularly will lower our billing weight.', 'C': 'Enabling ferry.eager will double the billing weight of the tiles in the receiving lane.', 'D': 'Splitting one lane into several lanes will never reduce billing weight.'}
rationale: ledger.compact only reduces stored history and does not reduce billing weight, while the other three statements match the reference.

stem: An unpinned Tessellate 4 lane already contains 7 tiles. An operator submits an 8th tile to the same lane. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The 8th tile is rejected with a capacity error.', 'B': 'The 8th tile is silently queued, and no error or warning is raised.', 'C': 'The lane automatically splits into two lanes so that all 8 tiles can run.', 'D': 'The oldest tile in the lane is evicted to make room for the 8th tile.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, and an 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: Five Tessellate 4 tiles must exchange intermediate data with one another within the same beat. No tile may wait for a beat boundary to receive data. Which layout meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Place all five tiles in one pinned lane for guaranteed scheduling.', 'B': 'Place the tiles in two pinned lanes and connect the lanes with an eager ferry.', 'C': 'Place all five tiles in one ordinary, unpinned lane.', 'D': 'Place all five tiles in a lane named _shared to keep their data private.'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane share memory and an unpinned lane can hold up to 7 tiles, whereas a pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles, ferries copy data only once per beat, and an underscore lane never runs unless pinned.

stem: A Tessellate 4 tile is waiting at a gate. The run uses the default beat length. The gate was last checked at second 0 of the current beat, and the gate's named condition becomes true at second 5. When will the tile move past the gate?
options: {'A': 'At second 5, as soon as the condition becomes true.', 'B': 'At the next gate check, at second 40, about 35 seconds after the condition became true.', 'C': 'At second 200, when the next metrics sample is taken.', 'D': 'Never, unless a snapshot is restored so the gate is checked again from scratch.'}
rationale: Gates are checked once per beat, not continuously, and the default beat is 40 seconds, so the tile waits until the next check at second 40.

stem: Before a snapshot was taken, a tile had already passed a gate that waits for an external approval record. After the snapshot, the approval record was revoked. The operator then restores the snapshot, and the tile is blocked at that gate again even though lane memory looks correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The snapshot did not capture lane memory, so the tile lost its record of having passed the gate.', 'B': 'The tile lost its scope during the restore and can no longer read the approval record.', 'C': 'Restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, and the approval condition is now false, so the tile blocks again.', 'D': "The lane's pin expired during the restore, so the scheduler stopped checking the gate."}
rationale: Restoring a snapshot re-runs all gates from scratch, so a tile that was past a gate is blocked again when the gate's condition is no longer true.

stem: Lane `reports` has the `wide` scope because most of its tiles need to read every lane. A new tile must be added that, for least-access reasons, may read only the memory of its own lane. What should the operator do to meet this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Add the tile to `reports` and give that single tile a narrower scope than the lane.', 'B': 'Add the tile to `reports` and enable the `trace` flag so that its reads are recorded and can be audited.', 'C': 'Add the tile to a new lane named `_reports_restricted` so that the scheduler hides it from other lanes.', 'D': 'Place the tile in a separate lane that does not have the `wide` scope.'}
rationale: Permissions are inherited from the lane and a tile cannot hold a narrower scope than its lane, so the tile must be placed in a lane that lacks `wide`.

stem: A reviewer is checking access grants in a Tessellate 4 deployment that includes an `_audit` lane. Which of the following setups gives a tile more access than it needs?
options: {'A': 'A tile that only needs to read memory from other tiles in its own lane has been granted the `wide` scope.', 'B': 'A tile reads memory from another tile in the same lane, and no extra scope has been granted.', 'C': 'A tile receives data from a different lane through a ferry, and no extra scope has been granted.', 'D': 'A tile that must read every lane, including `_audit`, has been granted the `wide` scope.'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane already share memory, so granting `wide` adds unneeded access to every lane, including underscore lanes such as `_audit`.

stem: A snapshot is taken while a 3 MB ferry is partway through delivering its shards from lane `ingest` to lane `score`. Several tiles in `score` had already passed their gates. The operator later restores this snapshot. What does the restore produce?
options: {'A': 'Lane memory as it was at the snapshot, plus the in-flight ferry shards reassembled in their correct order.', 'B': 'Lane memory as it was at the snapshot, with no in-flight ferry shards, and every gate evaluated again from scratch.', 'C': 'Lane memory as it was at the snapshot, plus the in-flight ferry shards, which may be out of order because Tessellate does not reorder shards.', 'D': 'Only the ferry contents in transit, because lane memory is rebuilt from the ledger after a restore.'}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, and restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch.

stem: An operator takes a snapshot while a ferry is still copying a batch of records from lane `orders` to lane `invoices`. After the snapshot is restored, lane `invoices` is missing that batch, but every other piece of lane memory is intact. What explains the missing batch?
options: {'A': 'The `trace` flag was off, so the batch was never recorded.', 'B': 'Lane `invoices` already held 7 tiles, so the batch was silently queued.', 'C': "A retry reused the tile's original inputs, so the batch was replaced with older data.", 'D': 'Snapshots do not capture ferry contents that are in transit, so the batch was not part of the snapshot.'}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, so data still on the ferry when the snapshot was taken is absent after the restore.

stem: A tile intermittently produces a wrong result, and the team needs to inspect the actual output it produced when it failed. Which approach will capture that output?
options: {'A': 'Turn on the `trace` flag for the tile and read the trace after the next failure.', 'B': 'Raise `retry.limit` so the tile fails more often and the output appears in the metrics.', 'C': 'Have the tile write its result into lane memory and capture that memory with a snapshot.', 'D': 'Rely on the metrics dashboard, which records tile results on every beat.'}
rationale: The `trace` flag records tile inputs only, never outputs, and metrics are only sampled every 5th beat, but snapshots do capture lane memory, so a result written to lane memory can be inspected.

stem: A tile in a pinned lane spiked in memory use on beat 12 and was back to normal by beat 13. The tile's run log confirms that it ran on beats 11, 12 and 13. The metrics dashboard shows no sign of the spike. Beats are counted from beat 1. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': 'Metrics are sampled only on every 5th beat (beats 5, 10, 15 and so on), so a spike that happened only on beat 12 was never recorded.', 'B': 'The pin expired after 12 beats, so the lane did not run on beat 12.', 'C': 'The `trace` flag records only inputs, so it removed the spike from the metrics.', 'D': 'A pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles, so metrics from the tile were discarded.'}
rationale: Metrics are sampled on every 5th beat, and events between samples are not recorded, so a spike on beat 12 alone falls between the samples taken on beats 10 and 15.

stem: Lane `_audit` is pinned, and its pin was renewed with `pin.renew` two beats ago. The operator now upgrades Tessellate to a new release. What happens to `_audit` after the upgrade if nobody takes any further action?
options: {'A': 'It keeps running on every beat for the remaining 10 beats of its renewed pin.', 'B': 'It keeps running indefinitely, because a renewed pin survives upgrades.', 'C': 'It keeps running, now with room for up to 7 tiles instead of 3.', 'D': 'It stops running, because the upgrade resets all pins and a lane whose name starts with an underscore runs only when pinned.'}
rationale: Upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, and lanes named with a leading underscore are invisible to the scheduler and never run unless pinned.

stem: No upgrade has taken place. An operator copied the key `pin.autorenew = true` from documentation for a newer Tessellate release into the configuration of the currently running version. The pins still expired after 12 beats, and no error or warning appeared anywhere. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'An upgrade reset the pins just after the key was applied.', 'B': 'The running version does not recognise `pin.autorenew`, and unknown configuration keys are ignored without warning.', 'C': 'The pinned lanes held more than 3 tiles, so the key was rejected.', 'D': 'Gates are checked only once per beat, so the renewal was delayed past beat 12.'}
rationale: Configuration keys that the running version does not know are ignored without warning, so the key had no effect and the pins expired after 12 beats as normal.

stem: Lane `ingest` ferries a 1.5 MB payload to lane `score` with `ferry.eager = true`. Lane `score` holds 5 tiles. Two of them do nothing, but the lane runs for 6 beats. What billing weight does lane `score` accrue over those 6 beats?
options: {'A': 'A billing weight of 30', 'B': 'A billing weight of 60', 'C': 'A billing weight of 36', 'D': 'A billing weight of 18'}
rationale: Under L1, billing weight is tiles × beats, and idle tiles in a running lane still count, so the base is 5 × 6 = 30.
