Under F3, an eager ferry doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane, so the total is 60. Option A (30) ignores the doubling. Option C (36) doubles the weight but leaves out the idle tiles. Option D (18) makes both mistakes.

stem: An operator ferries 3 MB batches of time-ordered records from lane `collect` to lane `report`. Tiles in `report` sometimes see the records in a different sequence from the one sent. Batches of 500 KB have never shown this. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'Batches above 2 MB travel as shards that arrive with no reordering', 'B': 'The 40-second beat is too short, so successive batches overlap in transit', 'C': 'Eager mode is on by default and reorders deliveries to reduce latency', 'D': 'The larger batches overflow lane memory, so records are reread at random'}
rationale: Under F2, a ferry larger than 2 MB is split into shards. The shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them. This explains why only the 3 MB batches are affected. Eager mode is not on by default; it only changes latency and billing. Beat length and lane memory do not cause records to be reordered.

stem: A tile in an unpinned lane has `retry.limit = 6`. It fails on its first attempt. An engineer then corrects the upstream data the tile depends on. The tile keeps failing on every attempt. What happens during its retries?
options: {'A': "Six retries fire with back-off, each using the tile's original inputs", 'B': "Six retries fire immediately, each using the tile's original inputs", 'C': 'Six retries fire immediately, each using the corrected upstream data', 'D': 'Three retries fire with back-off, each using the corrected upstream data'}
rationale: Under R2, a `retry.limit` above 5 disables back-off, so retries fire immediately. Under R1, retries reuse the tile's original inputs even if the upstream data has changed. The configured limit of 6 replaces the default of 3. Because the lane is unpinned, the failure only affects that lane.

stem: A tile failed because of bad upstream data. The data has since been corrected, but each retry still fails with the same bad values. Which action will get the work processed against the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Raise `retry.limit` so that later attempts reach the corrected data', 'B': 'Enable `ferry.eager` so that the retrying tile gets updates sooner', 'C': 'Submit a new tile so that the work starts from the corrected data', 'D': 'Turn on `trace` so that each retry reloads its most recent inputs'}
rationale: Under R1, retries reuse the tile's original inputs whatever happens upstream. More retries or faster ferries therefore cannot deliver the corrected data. Under O1, `trace` only records inputs and does not reload them. A new tile picks up the current data.

stem: Five independent tiles must each run on every beat for a 30-beat job. They do not need to share memory. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Pin one lane holding all five tiles and renew the pin before every 12 beats', 'B': 'Pin two lanes of three and two tiles and renew both pins before every 12 beats', 'C': 'Pin two lanes of three and two tiles once at the start, leaving the pins as set', 'D': 'Place all five tiles in an unpinned lane named `_priority` for scheduler favour'}
rationale: Under P1, a pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles, so the five tiles need two pinned lanes. Under P2, pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed, so a 30-beat job needs renewals. Under T3, underscore lanes are invisible to the scheduler unless pinned, so option D would never run.

stem: Lane `_reports` ran on every beat for weeks, kept alive by a job that runs `pin.renew` regularly. Last night the team upgraded Tessellate and added a new config key, `lane.priority`. Since then, `_reports` has not run. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The new version rejected the unknown key and halted lanes referencing it', 'B': 'The upgrade removed the pin, so the underscore lane is hidden from scheduling', 'C': 'The renewal job reached a limit on how many times one pin can be renewed', 'D': 'The lane passed the three-tile pinned cap and its extra tiles blocked it'}
rationale: Under V1, upgrading Tessellate resets all pins. Under T3, an underscore lane never runs unless it is pinned. Under V2, unknown keys are ignored without warning rather than rejected. The reference sets no limit on how many times a pin can be renewed. Under T1, tiles beyond a lane's cap are queued rather than blocking the lane.

stem: Lanes `parse-a` and `parse-b` each hold 3 tiles and run on every beat. Some of those tiles are often idle. The team wants to lower billing weight without dropping any work. Which change achieves this?
options: {'A': 'Run `ledger.compact` every night to trim the accumulated run history', 'B': 'Split each lane into two smaller lanes so that each holds fewer tiles', 'C': 'Enable `ferry.eager` between the lanes so their beats finish sooner', 'D': 'Merge the two lanes into a single lane holding all six of the tiles'}
rationale: Under L2, merging two half-full lanes into one lane reduces billing weight, and splitting lanes never does. Under L3, `ledger.compact` reduces stored history but not billing weight. Under F3, an eager ferry doubles the receiving lane's billing weight.

stem: A team is drafting a budget plan for Tessellate. Which of the following assumptions is wrong?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles in a running lane add nothing to the billing weight', 'B': 'Running `ledger.compact` trims history but leaves billing weight', 'C': 'Eager ferries double the billing weight in the receiving lane', 'D': 'Billing weight grows with both the tile count and beats run'}
rationale: Under L1, idle tiles in a running lane still count toward billing weight, so assumption A is wrong. The other three statements match L3, F3 and L1.

stem: A lane currently holds seven running tiles, and an operator submits one more tile to that lane. What happens to the new tile?
options: {'A': 'It is refused, and the operator receives a lane-capacity error', 'B': 'It waits in a queue for the lane, and no error is raised', 'C': 'It is placed in a newly created overflow lane automatically', 'D': 'It replaces the oldest tile, which is evicted from the lane'}
rationale: Under T1, a lane holds at most 7 tiles. An 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected. No overflow lane is created and no existing tile is evicted.

stem: Four tiles must pass roughly 5 MB of intermediate results to one another. The results must be read in the order they were produced, with minimal delay and no extra billing weight. Which layout meets these needs?
options: {'A': 'Put the four tiles in two lanes connected by an eager ferry', 'B': 'Put all four tiles in one pinned lane so they share memory', 'C': 'Put each tile in its own lane connected by standard ferries', 'D': 'Put all four tiles in one unpinned lane so they share memory'}
rationale: Under T2, tiles in the same lane share memory, so they need no ferry. Option D therefore avoids the out-of-order shards that ferries over 2 MB produce (F2), the beat delay (F1) and eager-ferry billing doubling (F3). Option B fails because, under P1, a pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles. Options A and C rely on ferries, which bring the shard-ordering problem. Option A also doubles billing in the receiving lane.

stem: In a Tessellate deployment that uses the default beat length, a beat boundary occurs at time t. A tile's gate condition is false at that moment. At t + 5 seconds the condition becomes true and stays true. When does the tile proceed past the gate?
options: {'A': 'Immediately, within a second of the change', 'B': 'At the following beat, roughly 35 seconds later', 'C': 'At the next metrics sample, up to five beats later', 'D': 'When the next ferry lands in its lane'}
rationale: Rule G1 says gates are checked once per beat, not continuously. Rule F1 sets the default beat at 40 seconds. The tile therefore waits until the next beat check, about 35 seconds after the condition turns true. Metrics sampling (O2) and ferry arrival (F1) do not trigger gate checks.

stem: Tile X had passed gate `schema_ready` and was mid-execution when a snapshot of its lane was taken. Since then, the upstream table that satisfied `schema_ready` has been dropped and recreated empty. After the snapshot is restored, the restored lane memory shows X's partial work, yet X sits blocked at `schema_ready`. What best explains this?
options: {'A': 'Restore rechecked the gate anew, and its condition is now false', 'B': 'The tile retried on restore using inputs captured before the gate', 'C': "The restore cleared the lane's pin, and unpinned gates re-arm", 'D': 'Restored tiles wait one full pin cycle before passing any gate'}
rationale: Rule S2 says restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, so a tile that was already past a gate can block again. The upstream table is now empty, so the condition is false. Lane memory (S1) is restored, but that does not exempt X from the gate. Retries, pins and pin cycles play no part in gate re-evaluation.

stem: Lane `ingest` holds the `wide` scope because several of its tiles must read the `_audit` lane. A new tile, `geocode`, is being added. Security requires that `geocode` be able to read nothing outside its own lane. Which setup meets that requirement?
options: {'A': "Add geocode to ingest and set the tile's own scope to narrow", 'B': 'Add geocode to ingest behind a gate that checks its scope', 'C': 'Add geocode to ingest and pin the lane, capping its access', 'D': 'Place geocode in a separate lane whose scope is narrow'}
rationale: Rule G3 says permissions are inherited from the lane, and a tile cannot hold a narrower scope than its lane. Any tile inside `ingest` therefore has `wide`, which per G2 includes underscore lanes. Only a separate lane with a narrow scope limits `geocode`. Gates control timing, not scope (G1). Pinning caps tile count, not access (P1).

stem: A reporting tile needs read access to lanes `orders` and `invoices` and nothing else. To save time, an operator grants it the `wide` scope. Which effect of this grant goes beyond the stated need?
options: {'A': 'The tile can now rewrite gate conditions in any lane', 'B': 'The tile can now launch ferries between any pair of lanes', 'C': 'The tile can now read hidden lanes such as `_keys`', 'D': 'The tile can now raise retry.limit for other tiles'}
rationale: Rule G2 says `wide` lets a tile read every lane, including underscore lanes. Underscore lanes are invisible to the scheduler (T3) but readable under `wide`, which is far broader than two named lanes. The reference describes `wide` as read access only. It grants no control over gates, ferries or other tiles' retry settings.

stem: Lanes `src` and `dst` are snapshotted together while a 3 MB ferry from `src` to `dst` is mid-transfer. Some shards have already reached `dst`'s memory, and the rest are still in transit. After the snapshot is restored, what does the system contain?
options: {'A': "Both lanes' memory as captured, minus the in-transit shards", 'B': "Both lanes' memory, plus every shard, reassembled in order", 'C': "Both lanes' memory, plus the in-transit shards in arrival order", 'D': "Only src's memory, since dst depended on an unfinished ferry"}
rationale: Rule S1 says snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit. The shards already in `dst`'s memory are restored, and the in-flight shards are absent. Tessellate never reorders shards (F2), so option B is wrong. Both lanes' memory is captured, so option D is wrong.

stem: Lane `extract` ferried a 1 MB batch to lane `report` a few seconds before a snapshot of both lanes was taken. After the restore, `extract`'s memory records the batch as sent, but `report` holds no copy of it. What most likely happened?
options: {'A': 'The batch was sharded and its out-of-order shards were dropped', 'B': "Trace was off, so the batch's outputs never reached lane memory", 'C': 'An earlier ledger.compact run pruned the batch from history', 'D': 'The batch was mid-ferry, a state snapshots do not capture'}
rationale: Rule S1 says snapshots do not capture ferry contents in transit. A batch sent seconds before the snapshot was still travelling between lanes, so it was lost on restore. At 1 MB the batch is under the 2 MB sharding threshold (F2). Trace only records inputs and does not affect memory (O1). `ledger.compact` affects stored history, not lane data delivery (L3).

stem: An operator needs to see exactly what value a tile produces on the attempt that fails. Which approach captures that value?
options: {'A': 'Turn on trace for the tile so each attempt is recorded', 'B': 'Write the result to lane memory and snapshot the lane', 'C': 'Read the result from the metrics sample after the failure', 'D': 'Raise retry.limit so failed attempts are logged in full'}
rationale: Rule S1 says snapshots capture lane memory, so writing the output there and snapshotting preserves it. The `trace` flag records inputs only, never outputs (O1). Metrics are sampled every 5th beat and can miss the failure (O2). Raising `retry.limit` changes retry behaviour and back-off (R2), not logging.

stem: A tile's memory use spiked to three times normal during beat 12 only, then returned to normal. The metrics dashboard shows no spike at all, and the collector reported no errors. What explains the gap?
options: {'A': 'The spike occurred on a retry, and metrics count first attempts', 'B': 'Metrics are withheld for lanes holding more than seven tiles', 'C': 'Beat 12 was not one of the beats on which metrics are taken', 'D': "The lane's pin lapsed at beat 12, pausing its metric feed"}
rationale: Rule O2 says metrics are sampled on every 5th beat, so beats 10 and 15 are sampled and beat 12 is not. Events between samples are not recorded. Nothing in the reference ties metrics to retries, lane size or pin status.

stem: Lane `ledger_sync` is pinned, and its pin was renewed with `pin.renew` at beat 10. At beat 11 the cluster is upgraded from Tessellate 4.2 to 4.3. What is the pin's state immediately after the upgrade?
options: {'A': 'Cleared, so the lane no longer has an every-beat guarantee', 'B': 'Kept, and it lapses 12 beats after the beat-10 renewal', 'C': "Kept, but the lane's three-tile cap is raised to seven", 'D': 'Kept, but it must be renewed again before the next beat'}
rationale: Rule V1 says upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, regardless of recent renewal. The lane loses the every-beat guarantee that pinning provides (P1) until it is re-pinned. The 12-beat expiry (P2) and the 3-tile cap apply only while a pin exists.

stem: On a cluster running Tessellate 4.1, an operator adds `ferry.compress = true`, a key documented for version 4.3, and `ferry.eager = true`. Afterwards, billing weight in the receiving lane doubles, but ferry payload sizes are unchanged, and no warnings appear in the logs. What explains the unchanged payloads?
options: {'A': 'ferry.eager supersedes compression, as eager ferries skip encoding', 'B': 'Compression engages just for payloads already split into shards', 'C': 'Compression waits for the next 12-beat pin cycle to take effect', 'D': 'Version 4.1 does not recognise ferry.compress and disregards it'}
rationale: Rule V2 says configuration keys unknown to the running version are ignored without warning. A 4.3 key therefore has no effect on 4.1. The doubled billing weight confirms that `ferry.eager` is recognised (F3), but the reference gives it no interaction with compression. Shard size (F2) and pin cycles (P2) have no bearing on this key.

stem: Lane ingest has 3 tiles. Lane reports has 5 tiles, 2 of which sit idle the whole time. Both lanes run for 6 beats. A ferry carries data from ingest to reports, and ferry.eager is set to true on that ferry. What is the combined billing weight of the two lanes?
rationale: Ingest contributes 3 × 6 = 18. Idle tiles still count and eager doubles only the receiving lane, so reports contributes 5 × 6 × 2 = 60, for a total of 78.

stem: A ferry carries a 3.5 MB batch of ordered records from lane parse to lane load. Records in load sometimes arrive in a scrambled order. A separate 0.5 MB ferry between the same lanes always arrives in order. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The beat is too short, so successive ferry copies overlap and interleave their records.', 'B': 'The larger ferry is split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not put the shards back in order.', 'C': 'Tiles in the load lane share memory, so concurrent writes race and shuffle the records.', 'D': 'ferry.eager is off, and only eager ferries preserve record order.'}
rationale: Ferries larger than 2 MB are split into shards, the shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them.

stem: An operator sets retry.limit to 6 on an unpinned lane. A tile in that lane fails because an upstream value was wrong. The upstream value is corrected a moment after the failure. What happens next?
options: {'A': 'The tile retries up to 6 times with increasing back-off, and the retries use the corrected upstream value.', 'B': "The tile retries up to 6 times immediately with no back-off, and every retry uses the tile's original inputs.", 'C': 'The tile retries 3 times, because the default limit overrides any value above 5, and the retries use the original inputs.', 'D': "The tile retries up to 6 times with increasing back-off, and every retry uses the tile's original inputs."}
rationale: A retry.limit above 5 disables back-off, so retries fire immediately, and retries always reuse the tile's original inputs even if upstream data changed.

stem: A tile keeps failing its retries even though the bad upstream data that caused the first failure has since been fixed. Which action will get the tile to process the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit to 10 so the tile gets more chances to succeed.', 'B': 'Set ferry.eager = true on the incoming ferry so the corrected data reaches the lane sooner.', 'C': 'Stop relying on retries and launch a fresh tile, so that it picks up the current upstream data as its inputs.', 'D': 'Turn on the trace flag so the retries record and reload the latest upstream values.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the tile's original inputs, so only a newly launched tile will read the corrected upstream data.

stem: A job has 5 independent tiles that never need to share memory. Every one of the 5 tiles must run on every beat for the next 30 beats. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Put all 5 tiles in one pinned lane, and run pin.renew on it every 10 beats.', 'B': 'Put the tiles in two pinned lanes of 3 and 2 tiles, and pin each lane once at the start.', 'C': 'Put the tiles in two pinned lanes of 3 and 2 tiles, and run pin.renew on each lane before 12 beats pass, repeating as needed.', 'D': 'Put all 5 tiles in a lane named _critical, and pin it once at the start.'}
rationale: A pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles and its pin expires after 12 beats unless renewed, so the job needs two small pinned lanes whose pins are renewed.

stem: Lane _reconcile contains 2 tiles. It was pinned and ran on every beat. Five beats after it was pinned, the cluster was upgraded to a newer Tessellate version, and since then the lane has not run at all. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The pin expired after its normal lifetime, and nobody renewed it.', 'B': 'The upgrade reset all pins, and a lane whose name starts with an underscore never runs unless it is pinned.', 'C': 'The lane exceeded the pinned-lane tile cap, so its tiles were silently queued.', 'D': 'A gate on the lane is now checked continuously and is blocking the tiles.'}
rationale: Upgrading resets all pins, and an underscore lane is invisible to the scheduler unless pinned; the pin could not have expired yet, because pins last 12 beats.

stem: Lanes A and B each hold 3 tiles, and each lane has room for 7. Both lanes run for 20 beats. An eager ferry (ferry.eager = true) carries data from lane A to lane B. Which change reduces billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact on both lanes after each run.', 'B': 'Split lane B into three single-tile lanes, each fed by its own eager ferry from A.', 'C': 'Merge A and B into a single lane of 6 tiles, so that the tiles share memory and no ferry is needed.', 'D': 'Pin lane B so that it is guaranteed to run on every beat.'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes reduces billing weight and also removes the eager doubling, which cuts the weight from 180 to 120; compacting, splitting and pinning do not reduce it.

stem: A team lists four assumptions about Tessellate costs. Which assumption is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles in a running lane still add to billing weight.', 'B': 'Running ledger.compact every month will lower our billing weight.', 'C': 'Combining two half-full lanes into one lane will lower our billing weight.', 'D': 'Turning on ferry.eager doubles the billing weight of the tiles in the receiving lane.'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight.

stem: An unpinned lane already holds 7 tiles. A script submits 2 more tiles to that same lane. What happens?
options: {'A': 'Both new tiles are rejected, and the script receives a capacity error.', 'B': 'Tessellate creates an overflow lane automatically and places the 2 new tiles there.', 'C': 'The 2 oldest tiles are evicted to make room for the new ones.', 'D': 'The 2 new tiles are queued silently, without any error.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, and any extra tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: Six tiles exchange about 10 MB of ordered intermediate data with each other on every beat. Three reporting tiles need only a final summary of under 1 MB. Which layout keeps the intermediate data correct and lets every tile run?
options: {'A': 'Put all 9 tiles in one unpinned lane, so that every tile shares memory.', 'B': 'Put the 6 working tiles in one unpinned lane, and put the 3 reporting tiles in a second lane fed by a ferry that carries the summary.', 'C': 'Spread the 6 working tiles across two lanes of 3, connected by a ferry for the intermediate data, and put the reporting tiles in a third lane.', 'D': 'Put the 6 working tiles in one pinned lane, and put the 3 reporting tiles in a lane named _reports fed by a ferry.'}
rationale: Six tiles fit in one lane and can share memory there, and a small summary ferry under 2 MB avoids out-of-order shards; a 9-tile lane silently queues 2 tiles, splitting the workers creates a sharded 10 MB ferry, and a pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles.

stem: A Tessellate 4 cluster uses the default beat length. A tile sits behind a gate whose condition is 'flag ready is true'. The gate is checked at t = 0 s, when the flag is false. The flag becomes true at t = 3 s and is cleared back to false at t = 30 s. No other changes occur. What happens to the tile at the next gate check?
options: {'A': 'Nothing happens at the next check, because the tile was already released at t = 3 s when the flag became true.', 'B': 'The tile is released at t = 40 s, because the gate remembers that the condition was true during the beat.', 'C': 'The tile remains blocked at t = 40 s, because the gate only evaluates the condition at that instant, when the flag is false.', 'D': 'The tile is failed and retried, because its gate condition changed state twice within a single beat.'}
rationale: Gates are checked once per beat (default 40 seconds) rather than continuously, so a condition that is true only between checks is never observed.

stem: A tile in lane 'publish' passed its gate 'upstream_done' on beat 20 and was mid-way through its work when an operator took a snapshot. Later the operator restored that snapshot. The publish lane's memory came back intact, but the tile is now blocked at 'upstream_done', and the upstream lane has not yet produced its completion signal in the restored run. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: {'A': 'The snapshot recorded the tile as blocked, because snapshots save gate state from the beat before they are taken.', 'B': 'The gate state was carried in a ferry and was lost, because snapshots do not capture ferry contents in transit.', 'C': "Restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, and 'upstream_done' is currently false, so the tile blocks again.", 'D': "The restore triggered a retry, and retries reuse the tile's original inputs, which predate the gate passing."}
rationale: Restoring a snapshot re-evaluates gates from scratch, so a tile that was past a gate blocks again if the condition is currently false.

stem: Lane 'reports' has the 'wide' scope because several of its tiles legitimately need to read many lanes. A new tile, 'summary', will be added to this workload. It needs only the output of one 'reports' tile, and a compliance rule says it must not be able to read the '_audit' lane. Which approach meets the requirement with the least access?
options: {'A': "Add 'summary' to 'reports' and assign the tile itself a narrower scope that excludes '_audit'.", 'B': "Put 'summary' in its own lane without the 'wide' scope, and deliver the data it needs through a ferry.", 'C': "Add 'summary' to 'reports' and rely on the leading underscore, since underscore lanes cannot be read by any tile.", 'D': "Rename '_audit' to 'audit' so that ordinary lane scoping applies to it, then add 'summary' to 'reports'."}
rationale: A tile inherits its lane's permissions and cannot hold a narrower scope, so the only way to restrict 'summary' is a separate non-wide lane, fed by a ferry, which is the only way to move data between lanes.

stem: An operator needs one tile in lane 'billing' to read lane 'orders', so they grant the 'billing' lane the 'wide' scope. The lane contains five tiles, and the cluster also has a lane called '_audit'. Which statement correctly identifies why this grant is over-broad?
options: {'A': "Only the one tile that needs 'orders' gains 'wide' access, but that tile can now read every visible lane.", 'B': "All five tiles in 'billing' can now read every lane, including '_audit'.", 'C': "All five tiles can now read every visible lane, but '_audit' stays protected because underscore lanes are hidden.", 'D': "The grant doubles the billing weight of every tile in 'billing', so it is over-broad in cost rather than in access."}
rationale: Permissions are inherited from the lane, and 'wide' allows reading every lane, including underscore lanes, so every tile in 'billing' gains access to '_audit'.

stem: At the moment a snapshot is taken, three things are true. Lane 'ingest' holds a parsed batch in memory. A 3 MB ferry from 'ingest' to 'enrich' is in transit as shards. A tile in 'enrich' has already passed its gate. The operator later restores this snapshot. Which outcome should they expect?
options: {'A': "Both lanes' memory is restored. The in-transit ferry data is not restored. The 'enrich' tile's gate is evaluated again.", 'B': "Both lanes' memory and the in-transit shards are restored, but the shards may arrive out of order. The 'enrich' tile remains past its gate.", 'C': 'Only the in-transit ferry shards are restored, because snapshots capture data movement rather than lane memory.', 'D': "Both lanes' memory is restored, the ferry is re-sent automatically on the next beat, and the 'enrich' tile remains past its gate."}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, and a restore re-runs gates from scratch.

stem: Lane 'merge' receives records from lane 'collect' by ferry. An operator takes a snapshot, and a few seconds before it was taken, 'collect' had sent a ferry that had not yet arrived in 'merge'. After restoring the snapshot, the records in that ferry never appear in either lane. Nobody has run 'ledger.compact', and no pins exist. What explains the missing records?
options: {'A': 'The ferry was larger than 2 MB, and its shards were reordered on arrival, which corrupted and discarded them.', 'B': 'Snapshots do not capture ferry contents in transit, so the in-flight records were not part of the restored state.', 'C': "The restore re-ran the gate on 'merge', and gates discard any ferry data that arrives while a tile is blocked.", 'D': "The restore triggered retries in 'collect', and retries reuse original inputs, so they overwrote the sent records."}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, so data that was in flight when the snapshot was taken is lost on restore.

stem: A tile occasionally produces a malformed result, and an engineer needs to inspect that result after the fact. The 'trace' flag is already on for the tile's lane. Metrics are collected at the default sampling rate. Which approach will reliably capture the malformed result?
options: {'A': "Rely on the existing 'trace' flag, because it records a tile's outputs whenever the tile produces a result.", 'B': "Raise 'retry.limit' to 6 so retries fire immediately, letting 'trace' capture the output on a rapid retry.", 'C': 'Have the tile write its result into lane memory, then take a snapshot of the lane.', 'D': 'Read the result from the metrics stream, because metrics record every tile output as an event.'}
rationale: 'trace' records only inputs and metrics are sampled only on every 5th beat, whereas a snapshot does capture lane memory, so writing the output there makes it recoverable.

stem: Starting from beat 1, a tile in an unpinned lane failed on beat 7, retried, and succeeded on beat 8. The metrics dashboard shows no failure and no retry activity for that lane. 'trace' is enabled on the lane, and nobody has run 'ledger.compact'. Why are the failure and retries missing from the metrics?
options: {'A': 'Metrics are sampled only on every 5th beat, and beats 7 and 8 fall between the samples taken on beats 5 and 10.', 'B': "The 'trace' flag suppresses failure metrics, because it redirects tile events into the trace log instead.", 'C': 'Failures in unpinned lanes are not reported to metrics, because they fail only that lane rather than the whole run.', 'D': "The retries reused the tile's original inputs, so metrics treated the retried run as a duplicate and dropped it."}
rationale: Metrics are sampled on every 5th beat, and events between samples are not recorded.

stem: Lane '_reconcile' is pinned, and its pin was renewed on beat 10 with 'pin.renew', so it would normally remain valid until beat 22. On beat 15 the operator upgrades Tessellate to a newer version and makes no other changes. What happens to '_reconcile' after the upgrade?
options: {'A': 'It keeps running on every beat until beat 22, because the renewal carries over to the upgraded version.', 'B': 'It stops running until it is pinned again, because the upgrade reset all pins and underscore lanes run only when pinned.', 'C': 'It loses its pin but keeps running normally, because the scheduler now treats it like any other lane.', 'D': 'It keeps its pin, but its tile cap is raised from 3 back to 7, because upgrades reset pinning limits.'}
rationale: Upgrading resets all pins, and an underscore lane is invisible to the scheduler and never runs unless it is pinned.

stem: On a staging cluster running a newer Tessellate release, the setting 'gate.poll_seconds = 5' makes gates check every 5 seconds. A team copies this setting into production, which runs an older release. In production, gates still check only once per 40-second beat. The configuration loads successfully, and the logs show no warnings or errors. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'Production upgraded after the change was made, and upgrades reset all configuration keys to their defaults.', 'B': 'The key is unknown to the older production version, so it was ignored without any warning.', 'C': 'The key applies only to pinned lanes, and none of the gated lanes in production are pinned.', 'D': "The key takes effect only when 'ferry.eager = true' is also set, because gate timing follows ferry latency."}
rationale: Configuration keys unknown to the running version are ignored without warning, so a key copied from a newer release silently has no effect.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets ferry.eager = true on a ferry that sends a 3 MB payload into a receiving lane. The receiving lane has 4 tiles, and the operator expects it to run for 10 beats. With eager off, that lane's billing weight would be 4 × 10 = 40. What should the operator expect?
options: {'A': "Latency drops, the receiving lane's billing weight becomes 80, and the payload arrives as shards that may be out of order and are not reordered.", 'B': "Latency drops, the receiving lane stays at 40, and the sending lane's billing weight doubles instead.", 'C': "Latency drops, the receiving lane's billing weight becomes 80, and eager mode makes Tessellate reorder the shards before delivery.", 'D': 'The ferry is rejected because eager ferries cannot carry payloads larger than 2 MB.'}
rationale: Eager ferries double the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane, and payloads over 2 MB are split into shards that Tessellate does not reorder.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a downstream tile receives records from another lane through a ferry. When the ferry carries about 1 MB, the records always arrive in the correct order. When it carries about 5 MB, the records sometimes arrive scrambled. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': "The ferry beat is too short, so the second beat overwrites part of the first beat's data.", 'B': 'The receiving lane holds more than 7 tiles, so some tiles read the data late.', 'C': 'Ferries larger than 2 MB are split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not put them back in order.', 'D': 'The trace flag is recording outputs, and this changes the order of the ferry contents.'}
rationale: Ferries over 2 MB are sharded, shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate never reorders them, so only the large transfers come out scrambled.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile runs in an unpinned lane with retry.limit set to 6. After its first failure, an upstream tile corrects the data the failed tile depends on. Every retry still fails. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The tile retries 3 times with back-off, using the corrected upstream data, and then the whole run fails.', 'B': 'The tile retries 6 times immediately with no back-off, each time using its original inputs, and then only that lane fails.', 'C': 'The tile retries 6 times with normal back-off, using the corrected upstream data, and then only that lane fails.', 'D': 'The tile retries 6 times immediately with no back-off, using its original inputs, and then the whole run fails.'}
rationale: A retry limit above 5 disables back-off, retries always reuse the original inputs, and a failure in an unpinned lane fails only that lane.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile failed because an upstream tile supplied bad data. The upstream data has now been fixed, but the tile's automatic retries keep failing in the same way. What should the operator do so the work runs on the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit above 5 so the retries fire immediately and pick up the corrected data.', 'B': 'Restore a snapshot of the lane so the retries re-read their inputs from scratch.', 'C': 'Run ledger.compact so the retry history is cleared and the next retry reloads its inputs.', 'D': 'Stop relying on retries and launch a fresh run of the tile after the upstream fix, because retries always reuse the original inputs.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the tile's original inputs even after upstream data changes, so only a fresh run of the tile will read the corrected data.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane named _audit has 3 tiles. It must run on every beat for 30 consecutive beats. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Pin _audit once at the start, with its 3 tiles, and leave the pin in place for the full 30 beats.', 'B': 'Leave _audit unpinned with 3 tiles, because a lane with fewer than 7 tiles is always scheduled.', 'C': 'Pin _audit with its 3 tiles, and renew the pin with pin.renew before each 12-beat expiry throughout the 30 beats.', 'D': 'Pin _audit and add 2 more tiles to it, so the lane has 5 tiles to absorb the extra work.'}
rationale: Underscore lanes run only when pinned, pinned lanes are capped at 3 tiles, and pins expire after 12 beats unless they are renewed, so the pin must be renewed to cover 30 beats.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a pinned lane named _reports ran on every beat, and its pin was renewed regularly with pin.renew. Yesterday the operator upgraded Tessellate to a new version. Since the upgrade, _reports has not run at all, and no error was reported. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The upgrade reset all pins, and because _reports starts with an underscore, the scheduler cannot see it unless it is pinned.', 'B': 'The lane passed 7 tiles, so the scheduler quietly rejected the whole lane.', 'C': 'The pin hit its 12-beat expiry, because pin.renew does not work on underscore lanes.', 'D': 'A gate in the lane is checked continuously and is holding every tile in a blocked state.'}
rationale: Upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, and an underscore lane never runs unless it is pinned, so the lane silently stopped.

stem: In Tessellate 4, lane A and lane B each hold 3 tiles and are each half full. Both lanes run for 20 beats. They exchange data through a ferry that has ferry.eager = true. Which change will reduce total billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact after every beat so less history is kept.', 'B': 'Split the two lanes into four lanes so that each tile has more room.', 'C': 'Keep the two lanes, and set retry.limit above 5 so failed tiles finish faster.', 'D': 'Merge lanes A and B into one lane of 6 tiles, which also removes the need for the eager ferry.'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes reduces billing weight, and removing the eager ferry also removes its doubling of the receiving lane's weight, while compacting and splitting never reduce weight.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a team lists its assumptions about costs. Which assumption is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles in a lane that is running still add to billing weight.', 'B': 'Running ledger.compact every week will lower our billing weight.', 'C': 'Turning on ferry.eager doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane.', 'D': 'Splitting one lane into two lanes will never reduce billing weight.'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an unpinned lane already holds 7 tiles. An operator submits an 8th tile to the same lane. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The submission is rejected with a capacity error.', 'B': 'Tessellate automatically creates a second lane and places the 8th tile there.', 'C': 'The 8th tile is placed in a queue without any warning or error.', 'D': 'The oldest tile in the lane is removed to make room for the new tile.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, and an 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: In Tessellate 4, six tiles must repeatedly share an 8 MB dataset. The records must stay in order, and the cost should stay low. The tiles do not need to run on every beat. Which layout fits best?
options: {'A': 'Put all six tiles in one ordinary unpinned lane, so they share the data through lane memory.', 'B': 'Put each tile in its own lane, and connect the lanes with eager ferries to keep latency low.', 'C': 'Put all six tiles in one pinned lane, so the shared data is always available.', 'D': 'Put all six tiles in a lane named _shared, so other lanes cannot reach the data.'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane share memory, and six tiles fit under the 7-tile limit, which avoids out-of-order ferry shards, eager-ferry billing doubling, the 3-tile pinned cap and the never-run underscore lane.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane runs with the default beat length. A tile in that lane is held by a gate that waits for the condition "export_ready". The engine checks gates at the start of each beat. The condition becomes true 5 seconds after a gate check has found it false. Nothing else changes. When will the tile be released?
options: {'A': 'Almost at once, because gates react as soon as their condition becomes true.', 'B': "After 12 beats, because a gate only re-evaluates when its lane's pin is renewed.", 'C': 'At the next gate check, about 35 seconds after the condition becomes true.', 'D': 'After 5 beats, because gate conditions are only read on metric-sampling beats.'}
rationale: Gates are checked once per beat, not continuously, and the default beat is 40 seconds, so the tile waits until the next check about 35 seconds later.

stem: In Tessellate 4, tile Q passed its gate "approval_granted" an hour ago and had been running normally since. An operator then restored a snapshot of Q's lane taken after Q passed the gate. After the restore, Q is blocked at that same gate. The approval flag has since been reset to false in the source system. What best explains why Q is blocked?
options: {'A': 'The snapshot recorded Q as blocked because snapshots only capture tile inputs, not tile state.', 'B': 'Restoring a snapshot unpins the lane, and unpinned lanes must pass every gate twice.', 'C': "The restore put the lane back in the scheduler's queue as an 8th tile, and queued tiles wait at gates.", 'D': 'Restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, so Q is checked against the current false condition.'}
rationale: Restoring a snapshot re-runs gates from scratch, so a tile that was already past a gate is checked again and blocks if the condition is now false.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile in lane "reporting" needs data from lane "sales" and nothing else. Lane "reporting" currently has the wide scope because other tiles in it audit every lane. Security requires that this tile has the least access possible. Which approach meets the requirement?
options: {'A': 'Move the tile into a separate lane that does not have the wide scope, and bring the sales data to it with a ferry.', 'B': 'Keep the tile in "reporting" and set the tile\'s own scope to read only "sales", overriding the lane\'s wide scope.', 'C': 'Keep the tile in "reporting" and rename the lane with a leading underscore so its wide scope is hidden from the scheduler.', 'D': 'Keep the tile in "reporting" and pin the lane, because pinned lanes are limited to 3 tiles and lose the wide scope.'}
rationale: Permissions come from the lane, and a tile cannot hold a narrower scope than its lane, so the tile must move to a lane without wide scope and receive the sales data through a ferry.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an engineer needs tile "invoice_check" to read one other lane, "orders". To do this quickly, the engineer grants the tile the wide scope. The cluster also contains the lanes "_audit" and "_payroll". Why is this grant broader than necessary?
options: {'A': 'Wide scope also lets the tile write to every lane, so it could overwrite "orders".', 'B': 'Wide scope lets the tile read every lane, including the underscore lanes "_audit" and "_payroll".', 'C': 'Wide scope makes the tile visible to the scheduler in every lane, so it runs once per lane.', 'D': 'Wide scope doubles the billing weight of every tile in the "orders" lane.'}
rationale: The wide scope lets a tile read every lane, including underscore lanes, so it exposes "_audit" and "_payroll" when only "orders" was needed.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a snapshot of lane "ingest" is taken while a 3 MB ferry is moving data from "ingest" to lane "transform". At that moment, some tiles in "ingest" have already passed their gates. Later, the snapshot is restored. Which statement about the restore is correct?
options: {'A': "Lane memory and the ferry's in-transit shards are both restored, and the shards are put back in order.", 'B': 'Lane memory is restored, and every tile resumes where it was without re-checking any gates.', 'C': 'Lane memory is restored, but the in-transit ferry data is not, and tiles that had passed gates may block again.', 'D': 'Only the ferry contents are restored, because snapshots do not capture lane memory.'}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, and restoring re-runs gates from scratch, so previously released tiles may block again.

stem: In Tessellate 4, at 10:00:20 lane "A" finished writing a batch of records. A ferry began copying the batch to lane "B". At 10:00:30, before the ferry had arrived, a snapshot of both lanes was taken. After that snapshot was restored, the batch was missing from lane "B", although lane "A" still had it. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The ferry was larger than 2 MB, and Tessellate drops shards that arrive out of order.', 'B': 'Lane "B" was unpinned, and snapshots only capture lanes that are pinned.', 'C': 'The ledger.compact command runs during a restore and removed the batch from history.', 'D': 'The batch was inside the ferry when the snapshot was taken, and snapshots do not capture ferry contents in transit.'}
rationale: Snapshots capture lane memory but not ferry contents in transit, so the batch that was still moving to lane "B" was not saved.

stem: In Tessellate 4, tile "score" sometimes produces a wrong result. The tile does not fail. An engineer needs to see the exact value the tile produced on a run where the error occurs. Which approach will capture it?
options: {'A': "Have the tile write its result into its lane's memory and take a snapshot of the lane after it runs.", 'B': 'Turn on the trace flag for the tile, because trace records both the inputs and the outputs of each tile.', 'C': 'Read the metrics for the tile, because metrics record every value a tile produces on every beat.', 'D': 'Raise retry.limit so that each retry logs the output of the previous attempt.'}
rationale: The trace flag records only inputs and metrics are sampled only every 5th beat, but a snapshot captures lane memory, so writing the result to lane memory and taking a snapshot keeps it.

stem: In Tessellate 4, tile memory usage jumped sharply on beat 7 of a run and was back to normal by beat 8. The metrics dashboard shows normal values for beats 5 and 10. It shows no record of the spike. The metrics system reported no errors. What explains the missing data?
options: {'A': 'The trace flag was off, and memory metrics are only collected for traced tiles.', 'B': 'Metrics are sampled only on every 5th beat, so an event on beat 7 that was gone by beat 10 was never recorded.', 'C': 'The spike happened in an unpinned lane, and metrics are only kept for pinned lanes.', 'D': 'The ledger.compact command removed the beat 7 record from stored history.'}
rationale: Metrics are sampled on every 5th beat, and events between samples are not recorded, so a short spike on beat 7 does not appear.

stem: A Tessellate 4 cluster has a lane named "_audit". It runs only because it is pinned, and the pin was renewed with pin.renew two beats ago. The cluster is then upgraded to a newer Tessellate version, and no other changes are made. What happens to "_audit" after the upgrade?
options: {'A': 'It keeps running for the 10 beats left on its pin and then stops.', 'B': 'It keeps running indefinitely, because a renewed pin survives an upgrade.', 'C': 'It stops running, because the upgrade resets all pins and underscore lanes never run unless pinned.', 'D': 'It becomes visible to the scheduler and runs as a normal lane of up to 7 tiles.'}
rationale: Upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, and an underscore lane runs only while pinned, so "_audit" stops running.

stem: An operator on Tessellate 4 sets retry.limit = 4. They also add the key retry.jitter = 2s, copied from the documentation for a later Tessellate version. Retries in the cluster still fire with the normal back-off and no jitter. No warning or error appears anywhere. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': 'Setting retry.limit above 3 disables back-off and jitter, so neither is applied.', 'B': "Retries reuse the tile's original inputs, so retry settings such as jitter are also reused from the original run.", 'C': 'The jitter applies only to tiles in pinned lanes, and none of the failing tiles are pinned.', 'D': 'The running version does not recognise retry.jitter, and Tessellate ignores unknown configuration keys without warning.'}
rationale: Configuration keys unknown to the running version are ignored without warning, and the retry.limit of 4 is below the threshold above 5 that would disable back-off.

stem: An agent books meeting rooms with a tool called create_booking. The tool expects dates in the format YYYY-MM-DD. When the model passes a date such as '03/04/2025', the tool returns only the string 'Error'. Logs show the agent retrying the same malformed call until it reaches its step limit. Which change most directly fixes the root cause of this failure?
options: {'A': 'Lower the step limit so that the agent gives up sooner and reports failure to the user.', 'B': 'Raise the sampling temperature so that the agent is more likely to try a different input on each retry.', 'C': 'Make the tool return a descriptive error that states the expected date format and repeats the value it received.', 'D': 'Add a sentence to the system prompt telling the agent never to call a tool more than twice in a row.'}
rationale: The agent cannot correct a call it does not understand, so an actionable error message that names the expected format and shows the bad value lets it fix the argument on the next attempt.

stem: An assistant has two tools. One is named get_data and is described as 'Retrieves data.' The other is named fetch_info and is described as 'Gets information.' One tool queries the billing database and the other queries the product catalog. The model often calls the billing tool for product questions. What is the most likely cause of this misuse?
options: {'A': 'The tool names and descriptions are vague and overlapping, so the model has no basis for deciding which tool fits which request.', 'B': "The model's context window is too small to hold the definitions of two tools at the same time.", 'C': 'The sampling temperature is too low, so the model always picks whichever tool is listed first.', 'D': 'The API limits each request to one tool, so the second tool definition is silently ignored.'}
rationale: Models choose tools mainly from their names and descriptions, so generic, interchangeable descriptions that do not say what data each tool covers lead to wrong tool selection.

stem: A team uses prefix-based prompt caching. Each request contains a 40,000-token reference manual, then the conversation history, then the user's new message. To help the model reason about deadlines, the team recently added a line at the very top of the system prompt that states the current date and time to the second. Since that change, the cache-hit rate has dropped to nearly zero. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': 'The reference manual is now too large to qualify for caching, because caching applies only to short prompts.', 'B': 'The cache lifetime is too long, so stale entries are crowding out new ones.', 'C': "The user's new message changes on every request, and any change anywhere in a prompt invalidates the whole cached entry.", 'D': 'The timestamp at the start of the prompt changes on every request, so the prompt prefix never matches an earlier cached prefix exactly.'}
rationale: Prefix caching reuses only an exactly identical leading sequence of tokens, so a value that changes at the very beginning invalidates everything after it, including the static manual.

stem: A support application sends every request with three components: a large set of tool definitions and instructions that never change, a customer profile that stays the same for one customer's session, and the customer's latest question. To minimize cost with prefix-based prompt caching, how should the prompt be laid out?
options: {'A': 'Put the latest question first so that the model sees it immediately, followed by the customer profile, and then the static tool definitions and instructions.', 'B': 'Put the static tool definitions and instructions first, then the customer profile, then the latest question, with cache breakpoints after the static section and after the profile.', 'C': 'Put the customer profile first, because it is the most specific content, followed by the static instructions, and then the latest question.', 'D': 'Interleave the static instructions with the customer profile so that each cached block mixes stable and session-specific content.'}
rationale: Ordering content from most stable to least stable maximizes the length of the prefix that is reused across requests and sessions, and leaves only the changing question uncached.

stem: An email assistant reads incoming messages from arbitrary senders. It has tools to search the user's mailbox and to send email on the user's behalf. Testers show that a crafted incoming email can instruct the assistant to forward confidential threads to an outside address. Which mitigation provides the strongest protection against this attack?
options: {'A': 'Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to ignore any instructions that appear inside email bodies.', 'B': 'Require explicit user confirmation before any send action, and remove the send tool from steps that process untrusted email content.', 'C': 'Wrap each incoming email in clearly labelled delimiters so that the model can tell the email apart from the system instructions.', 'D': "Scan incoming emails for phrases such as 'ignore previous instructions' and discard any messages that contain them."}
rationale: Limiting what the model can do while it handles untrusted input, and gating side-effecting actions behind human approval, prevents harm even when an injection succeeds, whereas prompt wording, delimiters and keyword filters can all be bypassed.

stem: A research assistant works through these steps. Step 1: the user asks for a summary of a public web page. Step 2: a fetcher downloads the page's text. Step 3: the downloaded text is inserted into a prompt that also contains the user's private notes, and the model in that prompt can call a tool that makes arbitrary outbound HTTP requests. Step 4: the summary is shown to the user. At which step can an attacker most directly exploit prompt injection to steal data?
options: {'A': "Step 1, because the user's request could itself contain hidden instructions written by the attacker.", 'B': "Step 2, because downloading a public web page gives the attacker direct access to the user's machine.", 'C': 'Step 3, because attacker-controlled page text reaches a model that holds private data and can send it outward through the HTTP tool.', 'D': 'Step 4, because displaying a summary on screen lets the attacker read it remotely.'}
rationale: Data theft becomes possible at the point where untrusted content, access to private data and an outbound communication channel all come together in the same model context.

stem: A team wants to know whether a revised system prompt produces better customer-support answers than the current prompt. Which evaluation method gives a valid comparison?
options: {'A': 'Run both prompts on a held-out set of representative real queries, have graders compare the answer pairs blind and in random order using a rubric, and check that any automated grader agrees with human labels.', 'B': "Run both prompts on the example queries that were used to write the revised prompt, and count how often the revised prompt's answer looks better.", 'C': "Ask the model that produced the revised prompt's answers to rate each answer on a 1-to-10 scale, telling it which prompt generated each one.", 'D': 'Compare the average length of the answers from each prompt, and treat the prompt with longer, more detailed answers as the better one.'}
rationale: Held-out representative data, blind and order-randomized comparison against a rubric, and a grader validated against human labels together control for overfitting, bias and position effects.

stem: A team reports that its LLM-based classifier identifies fraudulent refund requests with 97% accuracy on a test set. In that test set, 97% of the requests are legitimate and 3% are fraudulent. What is the main flaw in treating this result as evidence that the classifier works well?
options: {'A': 'Accuracy cannot be measured for LLM classifiers, because their outputs are generated text rather than labels.', 'B': 'The test set is too large, and large test sets tend to inflate accuracy figures.', 'C': 'A 97% accuracy figure is too low for any production use, regardless of how the classes are distributed.', 'D': 'A classifier that labels every request as legitimate would also score 97%, so the result says nothing about whether fraud is actually detected.'}
rationale: With a 97/3 class imbalance, accuracy equals the trivial majority-class baseline, so metrics such as precision and recall on the fraud class are needed.

stem: A legal team needs answers to questions about a collection of contracts that totals several million tokens, which is far more than the model's context window. Each answer must quote the specific clause it relies on. Which strategy best meets these requirements?
options: {'A': 'Keep the first portion of the collection that fits in the context window, and discard the rest of the contracts.', 'B': 'Summarize the entire collection into a single short summary, and answer every question from that summary.', 'C': 'Split the contracts into chunks along clause boundaries with document metadata, retrieve the chunks most relevant to each question, and ask the model to quote the clauses it uses.', 'D': 'Raise the maximum number of output tokens so that the model can produce enough text to cover the whole collection.'}
rationale: Clause-aware chunking with retrieval puts only the relevant original text in the context, which preserves the exact wording that quotation requires, whereas truncation and summarization lose clauses.

stem: An application places the user's question at the very start of the prompt and then appends about 150,000 tokens of documents, which is still within the model's context window. Answers frequently miss facts that appear in the middle of the documents, even though those facts are clearly present. What is the most likely cause, and what is the appropriate fix?
options: {'A': 'The output token limit is truncating the answers, so the fix is to raise the maximum number of output tokens.', 'B': 'The relevant facts are buried mid-context far from the question, so the fix is to place the question after the documents or to trim the documents to the relevant parts.', 'C': "The documents fall after the model's training cutoff, so the fix is to fine-tune the model on the documents.", 'D': "The documents use a tokenizer different from the model's tokenizer, so the fix is to convert the documents to a different text encoding."}
rationale: Models tend to make less use of information buried in the middle of very long contexts, so putting the question after the documents or reducing the input to the relevant material improves recall.

stem: A team uses a model provider that offers an asynchronous batch API. Requests are discounted by about half, and results are returned within up to 24 hours. Which of the following workloads is the best fit for this batch API?
options: {'A': 'A customer-facing chat assistant where users expect a reply within a few seconds.', 'B': 'An agent loop in which each model call depends on the tool results produced by the previous call.', 'C': 'Re-labelling 300,000 archived support tickets with sentiment and topic tags for a report due next week.', 'D': 'A fraud check that must approve or block each card payment before the checkout page finishes loading.'}
rationale: Batch processing suits large, independent, non-urgent jobs where a delay of hours is acceptable in exchange for lower cost, which describes only the ticket re-labelling job.

stem: A developer submits 10,000 summarization requests as a batch job. The batch completes with no errors. However, many summaries in the database are attached to the wrong source documents. The developer's code reads the results file and assigns the first result to the first document, the second result to the second document, and so on. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': "Batch results are not guaranteed to come back in submission order, so results must be matched to inputs using each request's custom identifier.", 'B': 'The batch discount causes the provider to use a smaller model, and the smaller model confuses documents with one another.', 'C': 'Requests in a batch share a single context window, so content from one document leaks into the summaries of others.', 'D': 'The batch exceeded its 24-hour processing window, so the provider silently replaced expired requests with cached responses from other users.'}
rationale: Batch APIs may return results in any order, so pairing results by position rather than by custom ID scrambles the mapping even when every request succeeds.

stem: An invoice-processing service passes model responses directly to a strict JSON parser. Even rare parsing failures halt the pipeline. The model API supports several features. Which approach gives the strongest guarantee that every response conforms to the required JSON schema?
options: {'A': 'Add detailed instructions and three example JSON outputs to the system prompt.', 'B': "Enable the API's structured output mode with the JSON schema supplied, so that decoding is constrained to valid schema output.", 'C': 'Set the temperature to zero so that the model produces the same well-formed output every time.', 'D': 'Ask the model to double-check its JSON before finishing its response.'}
rationale: Constrained decoding against a supplied schema enforces validity at generation time, whereas prompting, examples, low temperature and self-checking only make valid output more likely.

stem: An extraction service asks the model to return a JSON array of all line items in a contract. For short contracts the JSON is always valid. For long contracts the output often ends partway through an object, with closing brackets missing. The API response for these failures reports a stop reason of max_tokens. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The input contract exceeded the context window, so the model could not see the end of the document.', 'B': 'The temperature setting is too high, which makes the model forget to close its brackets on long outputs.', 'C': "The model's tokenizer cannot represent closing brackets after a certain number of tokens.", 'D': 'The output reached the configured maximum output token limit, so generation was cut off before the JSON was complete.'}
rationale: A max_tokens stop reason means generation was truncated at the output limit, which explains why only long outputs end mid-object.

stem: A team is building a research assistant that answers open-ended questions such as "Compare the regulatory approaches to AI in three regions." The number and kind of subtopics vary greatly between questions and cannot be known in advance. Subtopics can be investigated independently, and the final answer must combine all findings into one coherent report. Which orchestration pattern fits best?
options: {'A': 'A fixed sequential pipeline in which the same predefined stages run in the same order for every question.', 'B': 'A single agent that is given every tool and investigates all subtopics one after another in one long context.', 'C': 'An orchestrator agent that breaks each question into subtasks at run time, sends them to worker agents in parallel, and synthesizes their results.', 'D': 'A peer-to-peer group of agents that message each other freely with no designated coordinator or final synthesizer.'}
rationale: The orchestrator-worker pattern handles subtasks that must be decided at run time, runs independent work in parallel, and provides a single point for combining the results.

stem: In a multi-agent system, the orchestrator has a long conversation with the user that establishes the target market, the budget and the deadline. The orchestrator then sends a sub-agent the instruction "Draft the launch plan." The sub-agent's plan ignores the budget and deadline, and it asks for details that the user has already given. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': "The sub-agent does not share the orchestrator's conversation history, so the orchestrator must pass the relevant context explicitly in the task description.", 'B': 'The sub-agent uses a different temperature setting from the orchestrator, which makes it disregard constraints.', 'C': "The orchestrator's context window overflowed, so the user's earlier messages were deleted from the provider's servers.", 'D': 'Sub-agents can only read tool outputs and are technically unable to accept natural-language instructions.'}
rationale: Sub-agents start with only the context they are given, so a terse delegation message that omits established constraints causes them to miss information the orchestrator already holds.

stem: A retrieval-augmented support bot uses only dense embedding search. It answers conceptual questions well. However, it often fails to retrieve the right document when a query contains an exact identifier, such as the error code "E-4471" or the part number "XJ-220B", even though documents containing those exact strings exist. Which change is most likely to fix this?
options: {'A': "Raise the generation model's temperature so that it explores more possible answers.", 'B': 'Increase the chunk size so that each embedding covers more text.', 'C': 'Switch to a larger embedding model with more dimensions while keeping pure dense retrieval.', 'D': 'Add lexical keyword search such as BM25 alongside the dense search, and merge the rankings in a hybrid retrieval setup.'}
rationale: Dense embeddings capture meaning but match rare exact tokens such as codes poorly, and adding lexical search in a hybrid setup restores exact-match recall.

stem: A company's internal assistant is asked about the current parental leave policy. The retrieval logs show that the top-ranked chunk contains the updated 2024 policy stating 20 weeks. However, the assistant answers "16 weeks," which matches an older public version of the policy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {'A': 'Retrieval failed, because the relevant chunk was not returned to the model.', 'B': 'Retrieval succeeded, but the model relied on its prior training knowledge instead of the provided context, which is a generation grounding failure.', 'C': 'The embedding model is out of date and needs retraining on the 2024 policy documents.', 'D': 'The chunk size is too small to contain a number, so the model could not read the 20-week figure.'}
rationale: The logs show that the correct chunk was retrieved and ranked first, so the error arises at generation time, when the model favoured its parametric knowledge over the supplied context.

stem: A document Q&A application sends the same 60,000-token reference manual as a prefix on every request, followed by a short user question. Answers are typically under 100 tokens. The time to first token is about 4 seconds, and the target is under 1.5 seconds. Which change is most likely to meet the target?
options: {'A': 'Enable prompt caching on the static manual prefix, so that repeated requests skip reprocessing those tokens.', 'B': 'Turn on response streaming, so that tokens appear as soon as they are generated.', 'C': 'Lower the maximum output token limit from 1,000 to 200.', 'D': 'Move the requests to the batch API to take advantage of its lower price.'}
rationale: The delay comes from processing the large repeated input prefix, which prompt caching shortens; streaming does not shorten the wait before the first token, the output is already short, and batch processing adds latency.

stem: Each request has 10,000 input tokens, of which 9,000 are an identical system prompt, plus 200 output tokens. Prices are $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Cached input reads cost 10% of the normal input price. Traffic is steady, so the cache stays warm and cache-write costs can be ignored. If the 9,000-token system prompt is cached, by roughly what percentage does the total cost per request fall?
rationale: The cost falls from $0.033 per request ($0.030 input plus $0.003 output) to $0.0087 ($0.0027 cached input plus $0.003 uncached input plus $0.003 output), which is a reduction of about 74%.

stem: A support agent has one order tool, get_order(order_id). The tool's description documents the order ID format with examples. Users usually supply only the email address on their account. Logs show the agent passing email addresses into order_id. The tool returns an error that restates the ID format, and the agent then either guesses IDs or apologises and stops. Which change most directly resolves this failure?
options: {'A': 'Expand the get_order description with more examples of valid order ID formats.', 'B': "Provide a tool that returns a customer's list of orders from their account details.", 'C': 'Make the invalid-ID error message longer and more explicit about the expected format.', 'D': 'Instruct the agent to ask users for their order ID instead of their email address.'}
rationale: The agent already knows the ID format. It fails because it has no way to get from the information users actually have to an order ID. Adding a lookup capability closes that gap. More format documentation or a longer error message repeats what the agent already knows. Asking users for an ID they typically do not have shifts the failure onto the user.

stem: An assistant has two tools. search_kb is described as "Searches for information." search_web is described as "Searches for information online." When employees ask about internal HR policies, the model frequently calls search_web and returns public, generic answers. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'Two search tools exceed the number of tools a model can reliably track at once.', 'B': 'The tool names use snake_case, which models parse less reliably than camelCase.', 'C': 'search_web is listed second, so recency bias leads the model to prefer it.', 'D': 'Neither description says what content it covers, so the model cannot tell them apart.'}
rationale: The model chooses tools from their descriptions. Neither description mentions internal or company content, so nothing points the model to search_kb for HR policy questions. Two tools is well within normal capacity. Naming style and list order are not meaningful causes of this behaviour.

stem: A service runs many worker processes. Each worker builds its tool definitions by iterating over a Python set of enabled tool names. The content of the tool definitions and of the long system prompt is identical across requests. A cache breakpoint is placed at the end of the system prompt. Usage metrics show cache-write tokens on most requests and few cache reads. What best explains this?
options: {'A': 'The tool definitions can appear in a different order per process, which changes the prefix ahead of the system prompt.', 'B': 'The system prompt is below the minimum cacheable length, so entries are written but cannot be read back.', 'C': 'The cache breakpoint must be placed on the first user message rather than on the system prompt.', 'D': 'Cache entries are tied to one network connection, so requests from different workers cannot share them.'}
rationale: Tool definitions come before the system prompt in the cached prefix. Python's string hash randomisation makes set iteration order vary between processes, so the prefix bytes differ and lookups miss. Each new ordering creates a fresh cache write. A prompt below the minimum length would not be written to the cache at all. A breakpoint on the system prompt is valid. Caches are not scoped to a connection.

stem: Each request to a product-help assistant contains three parts. The first is a 30,000-token product manual that is identical for every user. The second is a 2,000-token profile specific to each user. The third is the user's question. Which layout minimises input cost under prefix-based prompt caching?
options: {'A': 'Question, then profile, then manual, with a cache breakpoint placed after the manual.', 'B': 'Profile, then manual, then question, with a cache breakpoint placed after the manual.', 'C': 'Manual, then profile, then question, with a cache breakpoint placed after the manual.', 'D': 'Manual, then question, then profile, with a cache breakpoint placed after the profile.'}
rationale: Caching matches on an exact prefix. Putting the shared manual first and placing the breakpoint right after it lets every user reuse the same cached 30,000 tokens. Leading with the profile or the question makes the prefix unique per user. In layout D the breakpoint follows the varying question, so its cached prefix is rarely reused.

stem: An email assistant reads a user's incoming messages and can send email on the user's behalf. The main concern is that an attacker emails hidden instructions telling the assistant to forward private messages to an outside address. Which mitigation provides the strongest protection against this outcome?
options: {'A': 'Wrap each incoming email in delimiters and tell the model that the enclosed text is data.', 'B': 'Run a classifier over each incoming email to flag likely injection attempts before reading.', 'C': 'Add a system-prompt rule stating that instructions found inside emails must be ignored.', 'D': 'Have the user approve each outgoing message and its recipients before the send executes.'}
rationale: Delimiters, classifiers and prompt rules all depend on the model or a detector resisting the injection, and each can be bypassed. Requiring the user to approve outgoing messages blocks the harmful action itself, regardless of whether the injection succeeds in steering the model.

stem: A pipeline handles user-uploaded documents in four steps. (1) Text is extracted with an OCR library. (2) A model with no tools summarises the text. (3) The summary is handed to a second agent that can write to the company database, and this agent carries out any follow-ups the summary mentions. (4) A log entry is recorded. Which step allows a malicious document to cause unauthorised database changes?
options: {'A': 'Extracting the document text with an OCR library that may misread some characters.', 'B': 'Summarising the extracted text with a model that has no access to any tools.', 'C': 'Handing the summary to the second agent as a set of tasks it should carry out.', 'D': 'Recording a log entry after the second agent has finished processing the summary.'}
rationale: Text derived from an untrusted document becomes instructions for an agent that can make database changes. Injected content can pass through the summary and be executed at that point. OCR and summarisation alone cannot change the database. Logging happens after the fact.

stem: A team wants to compare two system prompts for a support bot. They will run both prompts on 300 real tickets and use a separate LLM as a pairwise judge. Which protocol gives the most trustworthy comparison?
options: {'A': 'Show the judge both responses in a fixed first-then-second order and tally the wins for each prompt.', 'B': 'Judge each pair in both orders, keep only consistent verdicts, and spot-check against human labels.', 'C': 'Have the judge score each response from 1 to 10 without a rubric and compare the two average scores.', 'D': 'Use the same model that generated the responses as the judge so it matches the expected house style.'}
rationale: LLM judges show position bias. Running both orders and keeping only consistent verdicts controls for that bias, and comparing against human labels confirms the judge's verdicts match human judgement. A fixed order bakes position bias into the tally. Rubric-free absolute scores are poorly calibrated. Using the generating model as judge invites self-preference bias.

stem: Over two weeks, an engineer repeatedly edited a prompt. After each edit, they reran a fixed 50-question evaluation set and kept the edits that raised the score. Accuracy rose from 62% to 91%, and the report states that 91% is the expected accuracy in production. What is the main problem with this claim?
options: {'A': 'Fifty questions are too few to calculate an accuracy percentage in any meaningful way.', 'B': 'Accuracy should be replaced with F1 because the questions have free-form answers.', 'C': 'A gain this large is unrealistic for prompt changes and points to a scoring bug.', 'D': 'The final prompt was selected using the same questions that produced the 91% figure.'}
rationale: Edits were chosen because they improved this specific set, so the final score is optimistically biased and does not estimate performance on unseen inputs. A held-out set is needed for that. Fifty items give a noisy estimate but still a valid accuracy figure. Free-form answers do not require F1. Gains of this size from prompt changes are plausible.

stem: Analysts need to ask questions about a contract archive of about 1.5 million tokens, far beyond the model's context window. Answering often requires combining clauses from different documents, for example an amendment that redefines a term used in the original agreement. Which approach best fits this need?
options: {'A': 'Per document, extract every clause relevant to the question, then reason over the combined extracts in a final call.', 'B': 'Retrieve the five chunks whose embeddings are most similar to the question and answer from those alone.', 'C': 'Summarise each document into a short paragraph once, then answer every question from the summaries.', 'D': 'Increase the max_tokens setting so that the model can read the whole archive within a single request.'}
rationale: Extracting question-specific clauses from every document and then combining them preserves exact wording and catches cross-document dependencies. Top-5 similarity retrieval can miss amendments that do not share the question's wording. Short summaries lose clause-level detail. max_tokens limits output length and does not increase input capacity.

stem: A user sends about 120,000 tokens of meeting transcripts, followed by a set of questions. The request succeeds with no errors, and the answers are not cut off. Questions about the first and last transcripts are answered correctly. Questions about transcripts in the middle are often answered wrongly or marked as not mentioned. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The input exceeded the context window, so the API silently discarded the middle portion.', 'B': 'The tokenizer handles transcript formatting poorly and corrupts text past a fixed offset.', 'C': 'Models tend to use information placed mid-context less reliably than at the start or end.', 'D': 'The output token limit was reached, cutting the part of the answer that covered the middle.'}
rationale: Weaker recall for material in the middle of a long context, with stronger recall at the edges, is a documented pattern. APIs reject oversized inputs with an error rather than silently dropping text. Tokenisation does not corrupt text at a fixed offset. The answers were not truncated, which rules out the output limit.

stem: A team runs four LLM workloads. Which one is the best candidate for a provider's asynchronous batch API?
